This function conveys the interleave structure of the C-groups, and it has been proven that the interleave projections of the 13 discrete orbits form a normal series with the interleaving number 2.

A novel markerless system utilizes a depth camera to calibrate and position a robot without relying on explicit markers, successfully adjusting the depth camera's viewing angle and estimating the end-effector's pose in 3D space, even in the presence of obstacles. This innovative approach leverages depth image filtering, robot joint movement prediction, and dynamic pose estimation through the prediction step, allowing for accurate adjustment and real-time 50 Hz execution on a standard PC. Comprehensive experiments, including simulations and real-world testing with a Puma 260 robot, have validated the efficacy of this method, demonstrating reliable and precise markerless end-effector localization in a variety of environments.

A new model is introduced to describe an interference effect in data analysis, which occurs when the value of a variable influences the treatment it receives. Under this 'K-NN Interference' model, it is possible to develop novel inference methods for the analysis of treated and controlled units. We explore how to detect interference in this context and provide formal definitions for different types of interference under the K-NN model. Moreover, we propose an adaptive detection method that utilizes data similar to its application in detecting novelties. Experimental data from two real-world settings have been used to evaluate the proposed methods.

Calculations of neutrino emissions from self-destructing dark matter particles within a neutron star are being re-examined, specifically within the framework of a single mediator theory. Researchers have discovered that mediator particles with no charge tend to increase the rate of neutrino production in the center of a neutron star by several orders of magnitude. This altered rate is attributed to the impact of 3-body collisions involving dark matter particles. Initially, the center of a neutron star is expected to exhibit a higher density of dark matter particles than its outer regions. As a result, the enhanced neutrino emissions could lead to a reduction in the estimated age of a neutron star. Conversely, the neutrino flux from a dark matter-induced event like the Big Bang itself may need to be reevaluated due to the increased neutrino emissions.

The ongoing UNIONS project, the most comprehensive optical survey to date in the Northern sky, has just released its Catalog of Filters, Instruments, and Sources, a massive dataset containing approximately 80 million distinct galaxy shapes. To effectively analyze this data, an efficient measurement pipeline is crucial. Unlike other popular methods, ShapePipe utilizes Ngmix's fast, real-coefficient Bayesian shape measurement approach, which leverages pre-trained neural networks for enhanced performance. The pipeline successfully measured shapes for every source in UNIONS without requiring initial training, delivering exceptional results. The verification was accomplished by comparing its measurements with those of the ShapeRack pipeline, which has a long history of implementation, using the 33.5 square degrees of strong lens subfields from the CFIS survey as a test ground. The comparison revealed a strong correlation between the two pipelines' measurements, which is in line with our expectations, given the excellent performance of Ngmix. As a result, we obtained average shape noise levels of 0.28 and 0.31, with reduced residual biases of 0.0083 and 0.0065 for the shear and peak density parameters, respectively. Using the measured shapes, we mapped the mass distribution of the massive arc-like structure at the heart of the CL0025+1726 galaxy cluster, which corresponds to the UNIONS subfield CL0025F01. The resulting 3D mass surface density map reveals a consistently oriented pattern that agrees with the second data release of the CF

A notable consequence of a finding made by Veech more than 50 years ago, relating to the Kronecker-Weyl theorem, has significant implications for the field of diophantine approximation as well as to the study of the mod $1$ continued fraction of quadratic form values. Notably, this consequence has the effect of refining existing estimates for certain quantities related to diophantine approximation, such as $ \Lambda (F) $ and $ \Lambda_{\mathrm{per}}(F) $. Furthermore, the existing proof of one of the outcomes presents an innovative approach by merging the ergodic theory of $ \mathrm{SL}_2(R)$-actions with a concept discovered by Weyl in the context of metrical theory. It has been observed that the established results hold not just for the group $ \mathrm{SL}_2 $ but for any given double covering of it.

We prove that for k-rational singularities on local complete surfaces, k-Du Bois classification follows. The proof relies heavily on Corti's example, demonstrating that locally factorial for such surfaces does not imply smooth. Furthermore, for hypersurfaces in k-rational surfaces, k-Du Bois and k-rational classifications are equivalent, which was already known for k-equivalent surfaces for d < 10.

We've discovered a relationship between magnetism and temperature in a specific type of crystal that's described by a complex mathematical model, which shows parallels with a well-known phenomenon known as Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless transition. To understand the model's behavior, we used advanced computer simulations to solve the system's equations. By applying strong magnetic fields, we observed the breaking of spatial symmetry in the spin arrangement, which is further analyzed through the application of two different scales to the spin angles. Consequently, we developed a theoretical framework that describes how the spin arrangement is structured according to the temperature and the magnetism in the fields. From this, we derived two equations that predict the spin arrangements at specific temperatures and magnetism levels. One of these equations has a visible crossover transition, while the other behaves in a disorderly manner that transitions into an orderly state as the magnetism increases. Ultimately, we found that the magnetism levels at which these transitions occur can be adjusted by varying the strength of the applied fields.

In ordinary shadow matter, a high-density form of ordinary matter exists in a dense state. Researchers have discovered that in the early universe, a brief period of non-relativistic quark-gluon plasma followed the Big Bang, which could potentially transform into quark stars with unusual properties. A more recent study has found that, due to strong interactions, ordinary matter can form a dense state with unique characteristics. This study has been expanded to investigate how this matter state might be stabilized by the formation of compact objects such as neutron stars. The findings suggest that this matter state could potentially be reflected in the stars' gravitational redshifts and rotational velocities. Additionally, the study has found that a variant of this matter state, incorporating axion-like particles and sterile neutrinos, is possible.

This study optimizes the execution time of the Goto Page algorithm, originally intended to identify pages on the English-language Wikipedia based on search queries. The optimized version reduces the algorithm's time complexity from linear (proportional to the number of bytes in the query) to constant complexity (specifically, 450 milliseconds with accounting for overhead). Additionally, the optimized algorithm demonstrates a 2.8 times speed improvement in comparison to the original implementation, and it also facilitates the detection of pages that do not exist on the site. The optimized algorithm has been successfully applied to the actual Wikipedia MediaWiki software in an experimental manner.

This research employs the Tsallis holographic dark energy model in two scenarios, 
non-complex and complex, to examine the dynamics of the universe from a quantum 
field theoretical perspective. The parameter $c$ in the Tsallis energy density is 
related to the cut-off energy in the quantum field by using the relationship 
$p=\frac{\beta}{\epsilon^{2\sigma}}$, where $\sigma$ and $\beta$ are 
quantum parameters. In the non-complex case, the model demonstrates acceleration, 
with the ultimate goal of infinite expansion. Conversely, in the complex case, 
three qualitative behaviors emerge, namely big bang, big crunch, and steady-state 
motion, with the latter representing a permanently expanded universe. By taking 
into account quantum effects, the research shows that the transition from the big 
bang to the big crunch phenomenon can occur within a finite timeframe.

The LAMOST time-domain survey, which employs a unique approach by combining time series and high-resolution follow-up spectroscopy, has successfully gathered data on 287,095 stars after three rounds of observations. These data, obtained through 16 $K$2 plates in the northern hemisphere, reveal variable behavior in 4,699,517 individual observations. A total of 337,444 stars have been found to exhibit repeatable activity over five epochs, and subsequent follow-up spectroscopy revealed an initial 1,044 active stars based on their H-alpha equivalence width. However, it became apparent that an additional 303 stars required reclassification as non-active stars. Furthermore, high-resolution follow-up spectroscopy has yielded an initial total of 35,855 stellar radial velocities. Nonetheless, it became necessary to apply a more stringent criterion to isolate stellar radial velocities and exclude 14,669 weak-line coronal stars. Nonetheless, these LAMOST time-domain survey data are poised to significantly contribute to our understanding of stellar magnetic activity and the evolution of young and active stars.

Previous research has suggested the use of SRAM-based TRNGs for generating randomness, primarily due to the instability of SRAM cells under varying voltage conditions. Nevertheless, enhancing the randomness effect while minimizing power consumption remains a challenge for such designs. This paper introduces a novel technique called TuRaN to increase the randomness of SRAM cells by reducing the supply voltage, thus aligning well with power reduction. The proposed system operates seamlessly with existing SRAM memories and generates random bits rapidly. The experimental results demonstrate that TuRaN enhances randomness up to 99.9% and achieves 30% power reduction with only a 5% increase in latency.

A basic building block for developing complex molecular circuits is the single-electron resistor (SER). Like conventional transistors, SERs can be either bipolar or unipolar, with the latter being particularly valuable in integrated circuit design due to its ease of manufacture. Using a self-consistent quantum mechanical approach, our study explores the development of unipolar SERs comprising three identical molecules connected to a metal electrode. We investigate the impact of different electrode materials and the manner in which molecules interact with each other, all of which affect the conductance and memory capabilities of these devices. We identify the requirements for creating a complete set of unipolar digital logic gates utilizing only molecular conductors, including those necessary for the creation of complementary digital inputs. Furthermore, we examine an alternative design involving a non-conductive molecule and demonstrate that it can function as a complementary digital logic gate when paired with an SER. This concept offers potential for the creation of highly scalable, memory-rich digital circuits solely comprised of molecular conductors.

A novel approach has been developed for evaluating multi-loop Feynner integrals based on a graphical representation called causal trees. This method enlarges the traditional single-scale expansion by incorporating an anisotropic scale treatment, allowing for a direct calculation from the bare parameter to a finite value of a scale, apart from one particular scale. The developed algorithm can compute two-scale Feynman integrals analytically. We apply this new framework to simplify the evaluation of planar double-mass-hard scattering scattering integrals, then use it to derive subtraction terms for momentum-spacetime-regularization. The method's limitations and potential challenges are also discussed.

Quantum states at any given time in a one-dimensional two-state quantum walk can be represented through an eigenfunction expansion, which involves the product of probability amplitudes and the complex conjugate of the eigenfunctions corresponding to the specified Hamiltonian. This applies to both discrete and continuous time models of the quantum walk. By setting the initial condition to a confined state within the range of $0 \leq x \leq L$, the recurrence of the quantum walk at time $t$ or $T$ can be explained in terms of the recurrence of the eigenfunctions at that time. Specifically, since the recurrence is governed by the absolute value of the squared module of the coefficients in the eigenfunction expansion, which depends on the specific form of the initial condition, the recurrence may not occur for all possible confined initial conditions as it does under unitary evolution. Furthermore, the total probability of finding the system in any of the states at or before time $t$ or $T$ is shown to be dependent on the specific form of the initial condition and equals the sum of the probabilities associated with each state in a perfect Gaussian distribution, which in turn equates to the normalized total probability of $1$. This confirms one of the key assumptions underlying the theoretical framework of the quantum search algorithm.

This study examines the composition of hybrid stars formed by neutrons, protons, and various other particles. The analysis combines the Sigma-omega-rho theory for a specific nuclear phase with two distinct quark phase models, and incorporates Maxwell and Gibbs conditions to analyze the phase transition. By analyzing mass-radius relations, a hybrid star's mass is predicted to be limited to twice the mass of the sun.

The behavior of light passing through a cavity in certain states can appear to slow down or speed up due to the interaction between light and the mechanical oscillator within it. This phenomenon has significant applications in both communication and measurement techniques. Researchers have explored the properties of light within a cavity that is connected to another cavity via an optomechanical double-cavity system, first in the standard context of quantum mechanics and then in the context of non-standard $q$-deformation. By applying $q$-deformation, the states of light within the cavities become more complex, increasing their clarity and enhancing transmission. This improvement comes from the combination of $q$-deformation and the ability to change the phase of the optical field. Our findings can lead to applications in areas like imaging and sensing, and may also contribute to understanding how $q$-deformation affects other aspects of physics.

In a model where an exotic particle with R-parity has a high spin rate, researchers have found that the Scissors mode can occur at a lower energy level than expected. This anomaly can serve as an explanation for an observed nuclear energy state. The Two-Rotors model provides a suitable conceptual framework for studying the Scissors mode. When the R-parity particle decays, it releases energy in the form of dense bands. These bands can interfere with the natural vibration bands in the nucleus, potentially causing an observed displacement in the nuclear energy state spectrum. The study reveals that the interference is most pronounced when the R-parity particle's mass is nearly equal to the nuclear mass. The study's findings align with experimental data showing an anomalous nuclear energy state, indicating that the concept has practical applications in understanding nuclear phenomena.

In thin films made from metallic transition metal oxides, the interplay between spin, orbit, and charge is particularly complex due to fluctuations in these quantities. These films have the added feature of disorder, resulting from irregular placements of atoms at the surface. This research delves into the effects of disorder on the fluctuations of spin and orbit, focusing on the properties of manganite ultrathin films. By incorporating quantum loops into the manganite's lattice structure, the research reveals how disorder impacts the'soft' magnetic properties associated with spin and orbit fluctuations. Experimental data on the magnetic response of manganite films supports the theory that disorder plays a significant role in the development of these'soft' magnetic properties. Additionally, the research suggests that orbit fluctuations play a key role in the instability of manganite films at specific frequencies. These findings shed new light on the underlying physics of manganite films and the role of disorder in their behavior.

The equilibrium properties of a laser-cooled ensemble in a one-dimensional optical lattice are being analyzed, incorporating optical radiation pressure as a non-conservative force. By deriving a general expression for the lattice site occupation, we examine the equilibrium distribution of atoms per site. Numerical calculations are conducted to investigate the effects of non-conservative forces on Frenkel-Hall statistics and the changes in entropy per particle as a function of temperature. Additionally, the impact of non-conservative forces is characterized by an effective temperature parameter, explaining the observed shifts in equilibrium distributions. This model can be applied to various systems, such as cold atom ensembles in optical lattices under resonance field illumination.

This study delves into the relationships among cryptocurrencies by analyzing their trading connections. It's interesting to note that as more cryptocurrencies emerge, their trading links with other digital currencies and traditional currencies develop as well. In contrast to traditional financial networks, the high-order correlations in the cryptocurrency trading exchange network are significant. The research revealed that the pairwise relationships are mainly driven by high-order correlations, especially when considering the trading volume's impact. Conversely, the long-term stability of the cryptocurrency market is primarily influenced by its pairwise relationships rather than its high-order structures.

The role of quantum fluctuations in the growth of particles in the atmosphere is still poorly understood and lacks theoretical backing. To shed light on this issue, the vibrational zero-point motion of small clusters composed of sulphuric acid and water molecules has been studied using an ab initio-based model, which takes into account the full potential energy surface and incorporates the cluster's internal degrees of freedom. By advancing the nuclear coordinates based on the underlying vibrational modes, it was found that increasing numbers of trapped molecules lead to significant structural changes, particularly the formation of ring-shaped structures containing 6 and acid molecules, which is beneficial for nucleation. Conversely, the presence of excess acid molecules causes the cluster to stretch and lose stability. These findings contradict previous classical simulations, which indicated that higher concentrations of sulphuric acid enhance cluster growth by forming stable dimeric structures. Consequently, it was observed that the accumulation of large amounts of sulphuric acid in water clusters leads to increased repulsion and reduced stability, contrary to the predictions of classical models.

We establish the definitions for a compact perception pair, compactifying a perception pair, and compactifying a space of operators invariant under group actions and non-expanding in nature. It's proven that the compactification of a perception pair corresponding to an expanding action is synonymous with compactifying the space of non-expanding group-invariant operators. Moreover, under certain conditions, it's possible to construct a compactifying space of non-expanding group-invariant operators through a straightforward perception pair interpretation.

In quantum systems, the thermal Hall effect serves as a means of detecting topological properties via the emergence of long-range topological orders. This phenomenon is often mimicked by gravitational systems as a consequence of the holographic principle, which assumes that a quantum system has a dual description given by a gravitational one. However, the equivalence between thermal Hall conductance and charge conductance does not translate into gravitational analogues when systems undergo transitions involving edge modes. As a result, we find that gravitational systems fail to capture the Einstein relations for Hall conductances in the presence of such transitions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the holographic duality does preserve the Einstein relations for Hall resistances in cases without edge modes.

In numerous cases, the inherent structure of data allows for significant reductions in the required number of parameters for a suitable model. This study examines how this data-driven dimensionality reduction is incorporated into the weights of neural networks during learning, with similar effects observed for both supervised and semi-supervised scenarios. We have found that many common neural network architectures consistently demonstrate a simplified representation of the input data, resulting in improved generalization performance. The mechanisms contributing to this dimensionality reduction are explored in detail, with empirical evidence suggesting that the following key factors influence its complexity: the interactions between non-linear layer widths, the linear transformations between layers, overparameterization, semi-supervised learning, and regularization through weight decay. Each of these factors has a quantifiable impact on the regularity of the solution, with various factors interacting and compensating for one another. By developing a systematic framework for analyzing the regularity of neural network solutions, we are able to provide a comprehensive explanation for this phenomenon, ultimately facilitating the integration of geometric complexity into neural network design.

A new, more precise determination of the measurements for four Wilson coefficients in semileptonic $b\to s$ transitions has been made directly from data collected by the LHCb experiment. This was done by analyzing $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays, accounting for the $B^0$ oscillations in the experiment's reference frame. The coefficients in question are $R_{K^*}$, which relates the Wilson coefficients $C_9$ and $C_{10}$, and the coefficients $R_{K^*(\lambda)}$ for $K^*(\to \gamma\gamma)$ decays, which are sensitive to $C_9$. The analysis used 9 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ of $pp$ collision data collected at $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV between 2010 and 2012. The results have been combined with a previous study of $B^0\to K^0\mu^+\mu^-$ decays. This combined analysis has allowed the determination of the amplitude's diagonal and off-diagonal components for several scenarios. The new measurements are as follows: $R_{K^*}$ is between $0.37$ and $1.11$, with a 95.5% confidence level; and $R_{K^{*(2\gamma)}(-)}$ is between $3.17$ and $7.53$,

Automated essay grading has been a persistent challenge in Natural Language Processing. This research leverages state-of-the-art transformer-based models to tackle this difficult task, which has long been solved only by traditional machine learning methods and ad-hoc solutions. To improve the accuracy and robustness of these models, we apply data augmentation techniques, such as sentence rearrangement, to boost performance. Our experiments are conducted across multiple datasets and establish a new state-of-the-art rating accuracy of 94.8% using a long context transformer model, surpassing the performance of similar models previously developed.

A new class of marginal dependence models is introduced that can capture
non-linear patterns of dependence among continuous variables, distinct from
the representations offered by copula models. Like copula models, these systems
use standard univariate distributions for the marginal units, but the proposed
models enforce a stricter limit on the marginal probability mass at 0. The
models can be extended to accommodate various types of dependence, including
independence, direct and indirect relationships, and cases where components have
conditional independence given other variables. A new estimation method is
developed to estimate the parameters of these models, along with a likelihood
ratio test to determine if a dependence relationship exists. The theory is supported
with simulations and applied to real-world data on household income.

A two-tiered model of social mobility spreads opportunities to younger generations based on the older generation's success, with a limited supply of opportunities allocated through a random process. To explain the observed distribution of opportunities and their relationship with the previous generation's outcomes, the model incorporates a dynamic theory of social mobility, which relies on the likelihood of younger generations achieving success being influenced by their family connections. The observed correlation in data can be replicated in the model by adjusting the parameters representing past opportunities and the likelihood of intergenerational connections, thus providing a theoretical explanation for the distribution of opportunities in a social mobility context.

We demonstrate that the non-relativistic connection between spin and statistics can be derived solely from the properties of parity, without relying on any non-relativistic principles specific to the Pauli equations. This is accomplished by first establishing a general criterion for the application of single particle wave operators, then deriving a spin algebra from the relativistic Poincaré algebra under the assumption of spatial reflection symmetry. From this derived algebra, we obtain the non-relativistic spin-statistics principle without depending on the Pauli equations. Furthermore, we derive the single-particle Hamiltonian from the relativistic kinetic energy, thereby confirming that the properties of parity alone are sufficient to establish the non-relativistic spin-statistics connection.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT scheme that supports concurrent and efficient anonymous transactions. The current RingCT protocol adds opacity to Bitcoin, but it suffers from performance issues and security vulnerabilities. Specifically, the use of homomorphic encryption in transactions leads to prolonged verification times. Furthermore, the delegation of verification tasks by miners can compromise the protocol's security, as illustrated by vulnerabilities in previous versions. Our improved RingCT protocol addresses these limitations by leveraging a new type of encrypted range to present values, thereby reducing transaction verification time and allowing for faster mixing. Additionally, our solution rectifies past delegated verification vulnerabilities and is presented in a fully transparent and publicly verifiable manner.

The ability of the COMIX matrix generator to produce consistent linear systems within a specific range is demonstrated, as verified by solving approximately 1050 randomly generated systems using various iterative and direct solving methods. A code packaged with MPI is used to generate diverse systems on multiple CPUs, showcasing the diversity of the generated systems through dimension, symmetry, and structure variations. These coded experiments demonstrate the reliability and performance of the COMIX generator, as its toughness in producing consistent systems is proven, particularly in solving structured linear systems which presents an alternative approach to the classic ILU decomposition. By analyzing the generated systems, the importance of choosing an appropriate solver for each specific system is emphasized, thereby highlighting the value of having a diverse set of reference systems, known as calibration systems, which can be used for calibration and validation purposes. Furthermore, this study showcases the reliability and accuracy of the COMIX matrix generator in tackling massively parallel direct solving tasks. A database containing the 1050 calibration systems is available for public access through a dedicated website.

The production of heavy vector bosons in high-energy proton-proton collisions is studied using state-of-the-art theoretical models. The calculation takes into account the latest data from the LHC, including a specific observation that the production rates for $W$ boson production does not exceed the standard model's predictions. The impact of additional complex parameters in non-standard models on the production rates is analyzed for different scenarios, considering the availability of existing and potential future LHC data. The accuracy of incorporating approximate factorization in triple gauge boson amplitudes is evaluated, leading to the conclusion that it suffices for most practical purposes.

In 2019, the Hebrew Universal Dependencies treebank was launched, however it experienced an unexpected decline due to the absence of further funding for maintenance. This paper announces the revival of this treebank and presents new data consisting of 4260 sentences gathered from various sources including news headlines, medical texts and social media platforms. This new dataset has been annotated in accordance with the UD standard and is compatible with the existing UD Hebrew treebank for seamless integration. Furthermore, a fully supervised parser has been developed to facilitate efficient parsing operations. The documentation and annotated data are freely accessible on our website for the benefit of the academic community.

We offer a proof of a dimension decrease theorem for subsets of $\ell_p$ with $1 < p < \infty$. This confirms a conjecture made by Olevskii and Sodin. Additionally, we provide a corollary that addresses the stability of $\ell_p$-isometry on incompressible subsets, which generalizes a result previously established by Kechris, Moch and Tsolomitis for finite subsets of $\ell_p$ with $1 < p \leq 2$.

As data science initiatives struggle to deliver tangible results to business stakeholders,
a key challenge remains: ensuring that data science projects maintain their momentum
and successfully complete the deployment phase. Traditional data science pipelines often
 overlook the complexities of collaborative work and the nuances of delivering models
in a real-world context, leading to project stagnation and abandoned initiatives. In this
paper, we introduce a framework that addresses these issues by providing a structured
approach to data science collaboration and defining best practices for long-term model
maintenance. By establishing a unified language and shared understanding among team
members, this framework fosters effective communication, promotes continuity across projects,
and helps teams achieve lasting impacts that benefit organizations and society as a whole.

Current density estimates of error-correcting code performance rely on theoretical density-evolution predictions or simulated density-evolution estimates obtained from various asymptotic theorems. These methods, however, fail to account for certain system characteristics like degree distributions in individual codeword components. As a result, existing models are unable to accurately predict the dynamic behavior of specific system components. To address this limitation, we propose a new approach that involves directly analyzing the statistical properties of repeated erasures in a binary deletion channel. This approach allows us to develop an accurate and scalable estimator of local density-evolution equations for any degree distributions in low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes. When applied to LDPC codes under repetitive, independent binary deletion channel scenarios, our proposed estimator yields precise density-evolution estimates within the error floor region. Additionally, our method may be adapted for analyzing error-correcting code performance under diverse channel scenarios, including multiple, independent repeat erasures, repetitive repeat erasures, and variable repeat erasures.

Modern computing systems rely heavily on networks to access digital services, making network security a top priority. Most current security solutions within embedded systems lack a comprehensive approach, only protecting specific aspects of the system. In contrast, this work proposes a comprehensive security framework for embedded systems, focusing on a novel and innovative solution that integrates static network access control and dynamic real-time intrusion prevention. This model can detect and intercept suspicious network traffic at the application level, protecting against unauthorized network access and intrusion. By employing a system-level synthesis approach, the security framework is simplified, making it easier to design and optimize for varying security requirements. The design's versatility allows it to be applied to different operating systems, enhancing security across the entire system, and is demonstrated using an evaluation test bed featuring Linux-based network traffic.

A critical component in the decoy state approach is the analysis of quantum key allocation. However, a novel attack targets the randomness of phase in the decoy state protocol by manipulating the qubit projective measurement, which also affects the quantum key generation system's randomness. Our study begins with enhancing the Hacking efficiency in the QKD system using a random phase parameter. We then examine the $I(Q)|\psi^+(ilde{\u})\rangle$ relationship and propose an anti-Hacking strategy, which aims to detect the man-in-middle attack by comparing $I(Q)|\psi^+(ilde{\u})\rangle$ and $I(Q)|\psi^+(Q)\rangle$. Furthermore, we discuss how anti-Hacking affects the evolution of the Hacking efficiency over time and propose an anti-Hacking channel to prevent this kind of hacking. Finally, we explore the options for generating random phases in practice, including the partial phase randomization method.

Recent studies have demonstrated the efficacy of large language models in processing in-context learning tasks through few-shot examples, with the best results achieved when trained on specific datasets. To optimize the use of pretraining data, we examined how shifting between corpora of varying sizes and domains impacts learning speed and accuracy in the NLPL-SST dataset for sentiment analysis. Our findings indicate that training on larger datasets before processing novel tasks accelerates in-context learning and often improves accuracy, but only if the tasks are similar to the pretraining data. Conversely, moving to tasks with different domains or on smaller datasets slows learning and lowers accuracy, although a model's performance may improve if it encounters tasks with more common domains or on datasets with larger examples. Our results indicate that a model's capacity to learn in-context is a double-edged sword: while it enhances performance when applicable, it also hinders it otherwise.

Galaxy cluster substructures are influenced by star formation history, which is controlled by the development and evolution of molecular gas. This gas formation is primarily determined by cloud collision efficiency, rate of cooling, thermal conduction, magnetic field strength, and orientation. By investigating the interaction of galaxy clusters with their surroundings, we examine how these processes affect the growth and decay of cold gases within clusters. By analyzing the cloud collision efficiency and factors that contribute to it, we develop a framework to study the development of galaxy clusters using hydrodynamic simulations. Our results indicate that gas fragmentation and exchange of material between clouds are mostly dependent on the ratio of cooling rate to conduction rate and the stiffness of magnetic fields, which affects the cloud collision efficiency and resulting galaxy formation history. Furthermore, our simulations show that an optimal level of cooling versus conduction exists, leading to highest levels of star formation. Additionally, regions with high magnetic field strength tend to have lower beta values and therefore lower gas fragmentation. We also observe that thermal conduction enhances the growth of cold gases but only in the presence of magnetic fields. At high levels of conduction, it leads to increased decay of cold clouds. Our analysis confirms that an optimal level of conduction exists to support efficient cloud fragmentation and star formation across a wide range of cosmic scales.

The discovery of the $Cabbiboated$ unitary matrix, responsible for quark flavour mixing, has been confirmed by numerous experiments over the years. However, despite substantial progress in the field, the underlying theory used to describe this matrix is still an area of ongoing research. This investigation reconciles certain requirements from two different theories, one being the breaking of electroweak symmetry and the other, a theory of the strong nuclear force known as QCD. By applying the rules of unitarity to the CKM matrix, we have determined how the different elements of the matrix change as the strength of interactions in QCD varies. Ultimately, our research has led to the development of a new unitarity constraint which is expected to be confirmed by future experiments.

We've calculated bosonic scattering cross-sections for complex structures in ten-dimensional open bosonic string theory. Two regimes exist: a 'weak' string coupling order and a'strong' string coupling order. Evaluating the cross-sections in the weak coupling limit reveals a $1/\beta^6$ behavior at high energy $\beta$, which aligns with an extension of Gross' conjecture. This relationship applies to all bosonic states. Furthermore, the cross-sections exhibit a $1/(1+\beta^2)^3$ behavior at low energy, indicating a dS-Poincar\'e equivalence. Moreover, the transition from the weak coupling regime to the strong coupling regime shows an accord with the duality proposal of Kawai, Lewandowski and T\"ulesko.

The influx of mobile data is escalating at a rapid pace, prompting operators to upgrade their networks to maintain quality. To accommodate growing demand, upgrading existing Base Stations is essential; however, due to space constraints at these sites, dense deployments may not be feasible. To address this challenge, Radio Access Technology can be enhanced to support deployments within densely populated urban areas. By virtualizing RAN, mobile traffic can be guided towards locations requiring higher data rates, and unsold spectrum can be repurposed for mobile networks, boosting efficiency. However, the virtualization of RAN and distribution of unsold spectrum require a deeper analysis of the core network administration procedures to provide maximum sustainability and minimum environmental impact of 5G networks. This paper focuses on designing core network administration procedures for sustainable and efficient 5G networks, and it proposes a new model based on Self-Organizing Networks (SON) to maximize the utilization of unsold spectrum while minimizing energy consumption by adjusting the virtualized RAN according to varying data rates across different locations.

The objective of zero-speech synthesis is to create a vocal performance without relying on existing transcription data, instead using only untranscribed audio and a large language model, it seeks to generate a synthetic voice. Comparing this to speech synthesis, the most notable difference is the absence of transcription data and the need to derive acoustic units from speech units for both speech and transcription models. Influenced by the success of certain neural network based approaches in other domains, we use an F0 (frequency) predictor to generate a more natural vocal characteristics. Our experiments show that the F0 predictor significantly improves the quality of the synthesized voice, with a high correlation of 0.83 between predicted and actual F0 values. Our synthesis model is the first zero-speech synthesis system to achieve a mean opinion score of 3.40 on the WSJ database, improving previous methods with a gain of 0.20.

Optimizing multi-agent motion planning is a crucial issue in autonomous systems, which can be solved using convex optimization when modeled as a specific problem. This paper proposes a new multi-stage algorithm that addresses the scale-up issue by dividing the large problem into smaller ones and re-optimizing coupled variables at each stage. To tackle the complex non-convex components of the problem, the authors utilize McCormick envelope relaxations coupled with trust region methods, demonstrating improved performance over existing alternatives using cognitive architecture and benchmark datasets. This advanced framework is then applied to a self-driving lane-keeping example.

A fundamental principle in thermodynamics is that heat cannot be fully released from a system. We investigate an analogous concept within the context of quantum theory, constraints on converting quantum states when resources are limited to a specific type. Specifically, we examine the quantitative limitations on achieving this conversion exactly and efficiently, focusing on a particular scenario where one party has a quantum state and the other party has a thermal state. Our results indicate that even with unlimited access to thermal resources, there is always some quantum frustration – a measure of inaccessibility – remaining. We precisely define this concept of quantum frustration and derive its lower bounds for specific scenarios, notably involving multipartite entanglement and stabilizer states. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these bounds apply to a broader class of conversions, including those involving dephasing and dynamical maps induced by non-unitary evolution. The connection to a long-standing open problem in quantum information is also explored.

We demonstrate that a coffee cup containing coffee can be reduced to a simplified model for analytical and numerical study. This simplified model consists of a nonlinear oscillator subject to periodic forcing, which we identify as a well-known mathematical problem. Despite the simplicity of this representation, the dynamics of this problem appear to be unresolved. Consequently, it is unclear whether the coffee in the cup will experience large-amplitude sloshing or remain stable, which has implications for avoiding spills when carrying coffee in the cup.

In the context of decentralized optimization over a graph with multiple agents, each running a machine learning model, we address the challenge of handling distributionally shift problems. By combining robustness in models and diversity in datasets, a new concept known as distributionally robust decentralized stochastic gradient descent (DR-DSGD) is developed. It can be realized via two methods: one using an explicit robustness measure and optimizing models separately, and another offering a fully decentralized solution utilizing only local neighbor communications. DR-DSGD is proven to converge optimally while requiring minimal additional computational and communication costs. Experimental results demonstrate improved performance over standard DSGD, particularly in model robustness and overall efficiency. DR-DSGD offers enhanced practical value as it empowers agents to optimize their local tasks while maintaining overall system performance.

We utilize the concept of hydrodynamic attractors to establish a universal relationship between initial energy states and the number of produced particles in high-energy collisions. By combining this with an in-depth model of energy release, our findings demonstrate that entropy generated before equilibrium is established naturally accounts for the common trend of decreasing particle production with increasing centrality observed in nucleus-nucleus collisions. Additionally, we calculate the energy density of the initial state and outline potential avenues to utilize our research to determine non-equilibrium characteristics of the quark-gluon plasma.

Using complex simulations of star-forming clouds, the process by which powerful jets form is studied under different magnetic field orientations. In one scenario, strong magnetic fields align directly with the rotation of surrounding material, leading to magnetically induced collapse. In another, highly magnetized clouds collapse uniformly. In both cases, powerful jets with speeds exceeding hundreds of kilometers per second emerge early on, connecting directly to the core. However, as these jets strengthen, their connection to the core becomes intermittent or completely breaks off in the first case, and in the second case, their speed remains consistent at around hundreds of kilometers per second. Later in the simulations, weaker jets with lower velocities appear and are found to be powered by small, isolated regions within the star-forming cloud. These areas have the unique ability to both produce and propel these lower-velocity jets. In contrast, the relationship between the high-velocity jets and these lower-velocity jets is found to be highly complex and not well understood. Furthermore, the existence of these lower-velocity jets appears to be completely dependent on the highly complex and delicate structure of the star-forming cloud, rather than the high-velocity jets. As such, it is found that the lower-velocity jets appear almost exclusively in the magnetically induced collapse scenario, rather than the highly magnetized one. This reveals a complex interplay between magnetic fields, the rotation of surrounding material, and the highly dynamic and unpredictable nature of the star-forming process, resulting in highly complex and difficult

This study investigates the issue of balancing performance and energy consumption in constrained nonlinear systems equipped with performance metrics such as optimal vibration reduction and speed adaptation. To address this challenge, we optimize controller gains by considering constraints on system response and actuation limitations, thereby reducing oscillations and avoiding maximum actuation limits. A series of nonlinear constraints are implemented to ensure acceptable levels of vibration and adaptation rates. Building upon the Scaled Gradient Method, we develop an efficient algorithm to solve the nonlinear optimization problem, yielding desirable results for a test system modeled by a rotating machine.

To evaluate the impact of solar pressure on Earth orbits, researchers have identified key resonance zones surrounding stable orbit types. To gain a deeper understanding of a particular type of resonance, we developed and compared multiple methods for computing the resonance frequency, ultimately finding that the simplest approach yielded the most accurate results. Notably, the resonance frequency was found to vary significantly in response to minor changes in the orbit's shape. Additionally, we investigated various numerical integration techniques for tracking the resonance impact and observed that the Lyapunov structure's orientation remains relatively stable over extended periods, largely maintaining its expected configuration.

By merging the techniques of first-principle calculations and the Tomonaga-Tani equation, we have developed a novel approach to modeling the interaction of light with matter in a completely non-relativistic framework. We have demonstrated the strict conservation of charge, linear momentum, and energy in our method by applying the Noether theorem. Furthermore, we have extended the models to describe both single and paired electron behavior and developed a formalism for deriving the HB model from first-principle calculations. We have tested the integrity of our models using a sample copper atom and demonstrated their effectiveness in reproducing the atomic spectrum of copper.

In a problem focused on category-level perception, we consider utilizing sensor data to determine an object's type, position, orientation, and geometric structure within a predetermined class of objects. For instance, recognizing a litter bin from a specific class might involve identifying its pose, shape, and any corresponding semantic landmarks such as handles or openings. We develop novel solvers to determine the best object poses based on 2D and 3D landmark data and demonstrate their applicability to a variety of challenging tasks, including deciding whether an object is in a specific state or if its design includes particular features. Furthermore, we explore robust object pose estimation in the presence of perturbations and find that simple methods can be effective, even with significantly distorted input data. Through a wide range of experiments, we show that our proposed variants of the PCTS solver outperform existing object recognition methods and demonstrate improved results for various object manipulation tasks and applications.

We develop the initial theories for estimating parameters of Cauchy distributions, including the mean squared error, bias, a method for constructing confidence intervals, and asymptotic distributions of the estimators.

A new statistical method is developed for basket trials to assess sample size in subgroups and share information across them. This is achieved through a Bayesian approach where each patient's response is analyzed as a binary event. By employing a non-informative prior on the trial's parameter, the posterior distribution of the success probability in each subgroup $\pi_j$ is generated. A sample size calculation formula is then formulated using the posterior distribution. Specifically, for a given subgroup $j$ in a basket trial with $n$ patients, the formula calculates the expected number of successes based on the prior's characteristics and the specified type I error and power levels. It is noteworthy that this method allows subgroups with events to estimate the population parameter $\theta$ and those with no events to estimate the background risk $\pi_0$. Furthermore, the method facilitates borrowing information between subgroups with no events and those that have experienced events. The method's effectiveness is illustrated via a case study examining two subgroups in a clinical trial testing the effectiveness of a new drug in (i) patients with cancer and (ii) those with immunodeficiency disorders.

High-performance motion systems that meet precise requirements often face limitations due to factors like parameter variations, which can make linear system models inaccurate. This leads to issues in achieving the desired motion, especially when trying to move quickly. Traditional control methods using linear system models can cause oscillations and even damage the system when the actual system dynamics differ significantly from the nominal model. Variations in system dynamics may be attributed to changes in system properties or external factors. This research introduces a new approach - LPV sequential loop tightening - that addresses these challenges by considering the actual variation in system dynamics. This innovative method improves the accuracy of system modeling and facilitates the development of more effective high-performance motion control systems. LPV SLT complements this by leveraging the actual variation in system dynamics to enhance performance. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through simulation tests involving a precise moving platform used in physics and electronics research.

We introduce a general framework for aligning partial point cloud views, which leverages consistent preimages under geodesic distortion. The framework is based on a novel, self-supervised learning Regress-and-Fuse strategy. This approach initially develops a point cloud feature extractor in a self-supervised manner using a contrastive learning method. Next, it creates a projector that maps this feature space to a latent space. Subsequently, the projector is fine-tuned to preserve the class structure of the latent space while incorporating the view information. We propose an iterative reinitialization process to refine the projector and implement the Regress-and-Fuse strategy. By combining projector estimates, we achieve precise 6-DoF alignment. The alignment accuracy and computational efficiency of our method have been rigorously evaluated and compared with other techniques. Notably, our method surpasses other learning-based methods in alignment accuracy while significantly reducing computational time by over 5 times, making it more practical for real-world applications. The associated code is publicly available at https://github.com/Chen-Yun/PRNet.

A nilpotent group is considered a variation of abelian group when the addition operation is modified to be non-commutative, with a specific nilpotency level determined by the length of its commutator chain. Among all classes of nilpotent groups, those derived from the generalized abelian Baumslag-Solitar groups exhibit the unique characteristic of having finitely many conjugating images in every nilpotent group of higher rank. Specifically, we find that this same group of generalized abelian Baumslag-Solitar groups demonstrates the $R_\infty$ property in all nilpotent quotients, thereby extending a previous finding by Munawee, Seaton, and Wilburt who had shown the presence of the $R_\infty$ property in all free nilpotent groups of ranks 2 or higher.

To explore the sensitivity of various colliders to instability in the Standard Model, we have created a parameter presentation, demonstrating how low-energy instability affects different particle pairs and masses. LHC, muon colliders, photon colliders, and future hadron colliders are evaluated for their potential to discover SM instability. Considering the influence of the material of which the colliders are built, we have incorporated a systematic approach to establish the minimum reach of each collider for instability in the SM. Notably, a 30-TeV muon collider built with advanced materials could become the initial detector of SM instability. Given its relatively smaller size and lower costs compared to other options, this could serve as SM instability detection in a more accessible facility. Additionally, we have found that photon colliders have a substantially reduced ability to detect SM instability, making other paths such as beam dump or low-energy runs essential if this instability is to be discovered at a photon collider. Finally, we have established that high-energy hadron colliders require higher minimum masses and energy to discover SM instability, once material influences are considered.

A new technique is developed to process time-sensitive data from ultrafast experiments using an approach based on optimization in a trajectory basis. This technique represents a dynamic system with a set of trajectories and treats time-sensitive data as a sequence of images, which are optimized iteratively to satisfy two conditions - the system's equations and a similarity measure for consecutive images. This technique is demonstrated by applying it to the analysis of ultrafast electron diffraction data from a molecular wavepacket in order to determine the potential energy surface of a molecule. It is shown that the technique is robust to noise in the data and can accurately determine low-frequency features of the potential surface up to a frequency of about 1000 THz.

The study provides the mass distribution profiles of $D^*$ and $D^*_s$ mesons derived from their Bethe-Salpeter wave functions. Utilizing the Cornell potential parameters, the calculations demonstrate that the quark contribution dominates in the mass of these mesons, whereas the string component significantly affects their spin and parity properties.

We investigate key properties of several types of Gelfand-Shilov spaces, which are characterized by the decay of their smooth functions and their Fourier transforms. The nontriviality of these spaces, specifically ${\Sigma}^{\sigma}_s$, is shown to depend on the values of $s$ and ${\sigma}$ being greater than 1. The nontriviality of another variant, ${\Sigma}_s^{\sigma}(\Gamma)$, is demonstrated when $s>1$ and ${\sigma}$ lies between 1 and 2. The nontriviality of ${\Sigma}_1^{2}(\Gamma)$ for any convex compact set $\Gamma$ in ${\Bbb R}^d$ is also established. The nontriviality of ${\Sigma}_s^{\sigma}$ for $1
 \le s < 2$ and ${\sigma} > 1$ when applied to the ball in ${\Bbb R}^1$ is not yet understood and presents an open problem. The text also presents short proofs showing that certain spaces are nontrivial based on a Fourier characterization and includes a nontriviality result for yet another variant of Gelfand-Shilov space. Additionally, the text applies these results to understand the nontriviality of elliptic Toeplitz operators with smooth symbols.

Deep learning-based segmentation methods typically rely on data from multiple sources, but training on extensive medical image collections is often impractical due to time constraints and resource costs. Real-world applications also present challenges in selecting relevant images for segmentation tasks. This study proposes a novel approach using CycleGAN and GAN to perform segmentation tasks without labeled data from one modality (e.g., MRI), while producing outputs compatible with another modality (e.g., CT scans). By utilizing CycleGAN for image translation and a supervised GAN for segmentation, our method achieves this goal. We tested this approach using abdominal MRI and CT scans, and the results demonstrate its efficacy in producing accurate segmentations.

Recent advancements in recurrent neural networks have enabled accurate prediction of future actions in various scenarios. Nevertheless, when dealing with unobserved variables whose interdependence with future actions needs to be anticipated, traditional RNNs fall short. To address this limitation, we developed an RNN variant utilizing Radial Basis Function kernels for feature mapping, allowing the incorporation of unobserved variables and their dependence on future actions. Experimental results demonstrate that this model surpasses the performance of conventional methods employing kernel support vector regression, kernelized RNN, and our previously proposed TimePerturbation RNN in predicting future actions.

We conducted an in-depth analysis of a remarkable stellar flare observed from AD Leo during 1985, comparing its ultraviolet to infrared spectra from 1650 to 6800 Angstroms. The analysis involved reversing the simulation process to understand the physical processes behind the emission. The grid of models we used covered log g = 4.0 to 6.0 and the effective temperature range of 8000 to 35,000 K. The energy distribution of the emission in the far-UV was best explained by a high temperature (~35 million K) with limited contribution from the accretion flow's condensation envelope. The visibility of UV lines in the spectra indicated that the quiescent atmosphere had an average density of around 10^5 cm^-3. The presence of a pre-flare chromosphere was also detected, along with findings that support the idea of shared energy distribution in multi-component flare models. The simulation showed that during the flare peak the emission was dominated by a very hot plasma, while as the flare faded the contribution of cooler components became more pronounced, especially in the near-UV spectrum. The model's agreement with the observed spectra was excellent across the 1650 to 3000 Angstrom range.

We conduct a study on the deformation theory of G2-instantons within nearly G2 geometries. By establishing that the G2-instanton moduli space is equipped with a Ricci potential, we demonstrate that the almost Hermitian structure on this space is conformal when the near-G2 structure admits a torsion that is a 3-form. Additionally, we show that the almost conformal structure on the G2-instanton moduli space is preserved under the action of the holonomy group of the associated connection when the G2-instantons are deformed via a process known as transverse rank 1 deformation.

A bounded linear operator, T, is considered C-normal if it satisfies a specific relationship with a given C*-algebra element C. In the context of function operators, this condition translates to a particular norm constraint involving the Volterra operator. This study extends this definition to weighted composition operators within the H^2 space and explores the necessary and sufficient conditions for such operators to be C-normal. These conditions are further demonstrated to be equivalent to certain properties of the involved weighting and mapping functions. Moreover, a specific characterization is established for C-normal weighted composition operators with integer weights.

We derive infinite families of $p'$-sequences, comprising $p$-core shapes with a maximum size of $p^2$, which are based on the fundamental grid of size $p \times p$. Furthermore, we discover a connection between these sequences and the result of random walks on the additive residue graph of $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$.

Specifically, our analysis reveals that the frequency distribution of certain nodes tends towards a uniform probability as the number of steps in the random walk approaches infinity, thus exhibiting a type of 'locality' distinct from the usual'small-world' characteristics.

Additionally, our investigation into the frequency spectrum of nodes at distance $d$ from the starting point leads us to hypothesize the existence of a maximum frequency value at $d = 1$, which we believe to be true for any $d \geq 1$, although we only prove it for $d = 1$.

Recently, point cloud models have gained significant attention due to their capacity for representing geometric data. However, the collaborative effort required between model and user during the training process in models like WaveNet and LPC is particularly labor-intensive due to the complex three-dimensional shape of point cloud data. We introduce an innovative class of recursive neural networks called TPC that applies a unique transformation to each dimension of the input sequence, producing desirable outcomes such as lower parameters, faster processing speeds, and enhanced generative capabilities. Our experiments demonstrate that the four-way recursive neural network outperforms other methods in predictive power and exhibits a clear progression in performance as the number of layers increases. When applied to the task of neural sound effect creation, the four-way TPC achieves an exceptional 87.5% completion rate and a superior mean rating of 0.8763 from human evaluators.

We're investigating media access methods for frequency-modulated continuous wave (FMCW) radar networks, focusing on Slotted ALOHA and CSMA. Our analysis shows that, in the context of FMCW radar, the traditional ALOHA method's efficiency increases due to each radar's wide-spectrum transmission duration, resulting in reduced collisions. We derive formulas for average throughput and packet delay, finding that only half of transmissions succeed. In response to this insight, we introduce a new Slotted ALOHA approach, ALOHA-D, which enhances performance by utilizing transmission opportunities. We further introduce hybrid media access techniques, including ALOHA-D/CSMA and Slotted ALOHA/CSMA, and develop associated models to optimize radar transmission schedules.

Recent advancements in microscale optics have enabled the observation of entwined two-photon effects that result from a single quantum interaction between coupled optical modes and paired matter-photon interactions. These effects can be explored through experiments utilizing the Hong-Ou-Mandel setup, where the overlap of entwined two-photon states can be examined as they pass through a beam splitter. Such experiments have demonstrated a distinct spectral features arising from a quasi-resonant $\Delta$-type entwining transition driven by a two-photon absorption process. This research presents an overview of the Hong-Ou-Mandel interference experiments that have been conducted to study various spectral effects associated with entwined two-photon absorption, including a $1/f$ noise phenomenon arising from fluctuations in absorption and the influence of Linéarly Coupled Cavity Effects. Ultimately, the analysis reveals that despite the existence of these additional spectral features, the absence of distinct changes in the HOM interference minimum pressure suggests that the primary source of the entwined two-photon effect is the $\Delta$-type transition driven by a two-photon absorption process.

We calculate the logical circle-equivariant elliptic cohomology of complex projective spaces derived from finite dimensional vector spaces over the field of complex numbers. This is accomplished by constructing a highly structured cohomology theory specific to the logical circle action, which is an extension of the elliptic cohomology theory in Granje\'o, Krahno, and Stolnick's research. Additionally, our findings imply that the univariant cohomology theory resulting from inverting all Hopf cohomology rings of the logical circle equvivariant Steenrod algebra surpasses the conventional elliptic cohomology theory in terms of structure. Moreover, the generated cohomology classes of the logical circle equivariant elliptic cohomology of complex projective spaces in degrees three and four correspond to superstring amplitudes that incorporate one gravity and two closed string sectors. Furthermore, the findings of this research can be interpreted as describing the generating series of the superstring low energy effective theory up to four derivatives in six-dimensional string theory.

Temporal knowledge graph inference involves identifying relationships between entities within a knowledge base that can be represented as vectors. Current vector-based approaches have demonstrated success but have several limitations, including the requirement for explicit statements in the knowledge base and the challenge of handling entities with multiple roles. To address these limitations, a new method uses low-rank and model-agnostic representations that do not rely on explicit statements or an entity's role. The method treats each entity as a low-rank vector and uses a unified set of latent variables to represent different entities and relationships. The initial low-rank representation is determined by analyzing the distribution of knowledge base data while ignoring role information, and subsequent vector transformations are focused solely on predicting relationships. The method's effectiveness was tested in experiments that involved analyzing knowledge base data from DBpedia and YAGO, and the results showed that it outperformed existing vector-based approaches in temporal knowledge graph inference.

The effect of ground sound was investigated by comparing the sound pressure levels measured on a hard ground surface and a porous surface covered with a thin layer of water. The experiment involved measuring the sound field using 16 microphones in a circular array on two different surfaces under conditions of significant ground effect. The findings showed that the sound pressure levels on the soft ground surface were 9% lower than on the hard ground surface for a freely propagating sound wave. When considering the ground effect, the soft ground surface exhibited a higher increase in sound pressure levels than the hard ground surface, by 3.5 dB. The underlying mathematical principle was also analyzed using the hemisphere method and Bessel functions.

Despite significant research in quantum nonlocality, explicitly linking technical capabilities to practical applications remains a challenge. Our study addresses this issue by developing a rigorous proof that in a specific quantum system, non-local interactions unambiguously demonstrate their crucial role in applications such as quantum communication, even when non-optimal correlations are considered. This achievement stems from a detailed examination of the relationship between non-local interactions and their practical applications, which reveals that these interactions play a central role in such applications as perfectly secure quantum key distribution and entanglement-based single-qubit measurements. Moreover, we find that non-local interactions enable the distribution of partially secret keys in a way that surpasses conventional secret key rates by a factor of at least $\sqrt{\rho_{\rm B}(1-\rho_{\rm B})}$, where $\rho_{\rm B}$ is the probability of measuring a base state. This factor significantly improves our understanding of the balance between security and efficiency in quantum key distribution and indicates that non-local interactions can significantly contribute to practical applications where suboptimal correlations prevail.

Building on previous work by Duque, van Suijkerbuijen, and Trigiante, we re-examine the concept of flat special lines within the Grassmannian, specifically in relation to SYM theories, and expand upon the findings regarding their relationship with the center of mass. Additionally, we apply these findings to the case of four SYM theories on the Grassmannian and Sasaki-Einstein manifolds.

A newly proposed hydrogen boride compound, MbHn ($M$=Li, Na, Nh=2, 3), exhibits exceptional electronic properties with emerging evidence of its potential as a superconductor when exposed to high pressure. To assess this possibility, we employed a first-principles hybrid functional plus van der Waals interaction calculation. The results show that Na3B8 and Li2B6 do not demonstrate significant superconducting properties when compressed at 240 GPa due to a high density of states at the Fermi level stemming from an unbound p-z component. However, Na3B8, exhibiting a lower density of states, displays a 5.3 K intermetallic superconducting transition at 230 GPa. To attain substantial superconductivity in hydrogen borides, we propose modifying their structures by incorporating nitrogen atoms to replace hydrogen atoms, thereby reducing the density of states and enhancing electron correlations. The calculated results indicate that Li3B8N2 and Na2B6N4 can exhibit superconducting transitions of 31 and 19 K at 230 GPa, respectively.

This paper examines the problem of distributing independent tasks to nodes in a distributed system, with each node capable of processing multiple tasks simultaneously. A new task allocation approach is proposed, which utilizes a simplified graph representation and applies a conventional graph coloring technique to determine optimal task assignments. To improve algorithm efficiency, the method is optimized for near-optimal performance. Experimental results are presented to demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed algorithm.

This article examines the characteristics of charmability and stiffness in arithmetic groups, particularly in the context of linear groups and commutator groups. It also explores their implications in shaping irreducible lattices and establishes certain unification theorems among aspherical lattices. Furthermore, the article introduces a new concept called 'characterness' to comprehensively understand and classify irreducible lattices based on their aspherical characteristics.

Highly automated driving systems designed for residual control in the event of a failure require a robust architecture that can handle human-machine interfaces and control modules working in conjunction. To guarantee the safety of such systems, our research team developed a model of operation for the fail-operative driving system, which includes an automatic reasoning process to identify and rectify potential weaknesses in the system design. By utilizing the SYGUSY tool for model checking and SMT probing, our results showcase the effectiveness of this approach in safeguarding the safety of highly automated drivers.

In the field of network dynamics, system instability frequently emerges and is often made public only after significant damage has occurred. To minimize harm, it's crucial to quickly identify the core elements contributing to instability in a given system. We introduce a novel data-driven approach called Impact Based Clustering, which pinpoints unstable nodes in a dynamical network and groups them according to their instability characteristics. The method's efficiency and accuracy are demonstrated through cluster formation times and overall cluster quality, outperforming traditional clustering methods. A case study of a financial network is used to showcase the approach's efficacy in real-world applications.

Recent research has centered on evaluating Leibniz's methods for handling infinitesimals
palely compared to the development of the formal theory of infinitesimals. This paper seeks
to alter the balance by examining the core concepts of Leibniz's calculus. Initially, we
will establish the fundamental principles of Leibniz's theory within the context of
microcontinuity, then apply these principles to regenerate his differential and integral
concepts. By employing a uniform approach based on the properties of sets, this study
maintains a strictly historical focus on Leibniz's original thoughts without incorporating
modern concepts like the transfer principle. Ultimately, the paper contends that a
microcontinuity-based framework offers a more accurate and versatile representation of
Leibniz's calculus when compared to the standard approach in both smooth and nonstandard
dynamics. Additionally, we have found that the latter method surpasses the potential of the
hyperfinite approach in nonstandard analysis in reconstructing Leibniz's calculus.

Large-scale cosmological studies are gaining traction through HI intensity mapping technology, which leverages the signal that HI radiation emits on large cosmic scales. Upcoming projects like CHORD will employ a phased array design to achieve high resolution and efficiency. A related study conducted noise analysis on a phased array with a circular footprint, comparing theoretical predictions with actual measurements from the data. After that, the researchers removed the bright foreground emissions from the data using a machine learning technique called Classification Image Logistic Regression, which models the noise as a function of the sky's structure and pixel intensity. The outcome revealed that the removal of foreground emissions introduces non-Gaussian noise with a longer tail, which significantly increases the standard deviation in the power spectrum's quadrupole and octupole modes by 4.4 and 1.5 times, respectively, in the frequency range from 100-300 kHz. The same removal process introduced analogous noise deviations in the power spectrum's different modes at various frequency ranges. Moreover, the removal of HI signal at scales larger than the beam size introduced noise with analogous deviation in the power spectrum at a scale of 100 Mpc. The current findings suggest that foreground removal could substantially impact the analysis of HI intensity mapping data on sufficiently large scales.

We examine the connection between the concepts of independence, extremality, and operator representability in relation to Hilbert space operators. Specifically, we explore how these concepts interrelate in the context of compact operators on an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space, revealing the distinct relationships between these concepts versus those on finite-dimensional spaces.

One key area in recent research, especially in e-commerce, has focused on addressing the issue of users' diverse preferences. A new hybrid approach combines document context-based and behavior-based collaborative filtering methods to improve recommendation accuracy. It first generates synthetic user profiles based on relevant document groups and then merges these profiles with actual user data to derive enhanced user preferences. Experimental results on JML dataset show that this method outperforms separate implementations of the individual techniques and a previous hybrid model proposed in 2008.

The concept of openness of type B is a conditional generalization of the concept of openness, applicable to functions with zero Newton strata at specific points. By adapting this concept, we examine the local behavior of truncated unitary invariant ensembles near their eigenvalues. We establish a novel criterion for a type B opening condition among the eigenvalues' empirical distribution functions. Furthermore, we explore the concept of conditional freeness for non-commutative stochastic processes. By incorporating these results, we obtain new insights into the local eigenvalue distribution of truncated unitary invariant ensembles and the resulting macroscopic matrix eigenvalue spectra. We also provide a detailed case study involving the Gaussian Chernovitz ensemble.

The problem of empty set uniqueness (PESU) in model checking has been addressed in a previous study, which established a relationship between PESU and the closure of a model-based zonotape representation under the intersection of an infinitesimal neighborhood and the complement of an infinitesimal neighborhood. Building on this foundation, a more general theory incorporating continuous time is developed in the present paper. It first introduces a new expression, timed empty set uniqueness (TESU), which subsumes PESU, and demonstrates its relationship with a model checking problem. A refined zonotape representation is introduced to express the finite reachability set of a timed transition system (TTS) using timed hypercubes (THs). Although THs are insufficiently closed under the desired transformations for TESU, a novel model checking algorithm utilizing an equivalence relation on finite paths is proposed, achieving linear computational complexity in the size of the TTS.

The decay reactions $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi f_0(980)$ and $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi
a_0(980)$ are examined in detail. It is noted that the measurement of the former
process by the LHCb collaboration shows a discrepancy with theoretical
predictions when incorporating the $a_0(980)-f_0(980)$ blending effect. A
new quark model calculation for the $a_0(980)$ resonance has been conducted to
address this discrepancy. When accounting for the blending effect and employing
this updated calculation, the theoretical prediction for the LHCb-measured branching fraction is
agreed with. Additionally, our study reveals that the direct $a_0(980)$ production
process dominates the decay reaction and allows for evidence of the $a_0(980)$
resonance through its dominant decays to $\pi^0 \eta$ or $\pi^0 \gamma$.

The GRAVITY instrument boasts four laser guide stars simultaneous in different directions, which are regulated by the NAOMI adaptive optics system on the Very Large Telescope Interferometer. Despite occasional losses, the NAOMI sub-system maintains high image stability, even when its four sub-pupils combine to form a single pupil.
