Deep neural networks (DNNs) have been highly effective in wireless localization assisted by channel state information (CSI), but they demand a considerable amount of labeled data and have complex architectures. This paper introduces a new perspective by employing sequence-to-sequence models to leverage CSI data, revealing that attention mechanisms can significantly enhance the performance of wireless localization. By incorporating attention-assisted CSI (AACI) data into the DNN, the need for labeled data can be further reduced. Our experimental results confirm that the proposed network achieves superior accuracy at a lower training cost compared to the conventional CSI-based approach.

This paper presents a comprehensive framework for modal logic semantics by linking different systems to the topology of their corresponding categories. Building on similar ideas expressed in the opaqueness hypothesis, we reveal the underlying structural properties of modal logic operators and their relationships with category topologies. The proposed framework allows a systematic approach to studying modal logic semantics through the use of diagrammatic reasoning, enabling the development of new modal logic systems and connections to existing ones.

A graph's edge coloring is defined as assigning colors to edges while ensuring adjacent edges receive distinct colors, with a minimum of Δ + 1 colors required for a full edge coloring, where Δ represents the maximum degree of a graph vertex. Considering bipartite graphs with cubic vertices, we investigate if a bipartite graph with cubic vertices and a maximum vertex degree of three can be edge colored using four colors. We present a counterexample, specifically the Grünbaum's 11-vertex cage, which cannot be successfully colored using just four colors.

This paper explores the minimum eigenvalue of the generalized Laplacian of the Hamming graph H(n,q) and establishes a function that depends on n and q. It also examines the extremal values of this function in relation to n and q. Furthermore, the results obtained from this investigation are compared with the findings from an earlier study by Alon and Mohar, which analyzed the extremal values of the second smallest eigenvalue of the Laplacian of a graph.

COPASI is a widely-used simulation and analysis tool for biochemical networks and their dynamics, but its desktop-centric interface may pose limitations for some users. To address this, we developed ShinyCOPASI, a web-based platform offering a range of new features and functionalities. This innovative interface leverages the capabilities of COPASI to provide a comprehensive range of tools, including data visualization, sensitivity and parameter estimation, and equilibrium analysis. By integrating these tools with interactive features, such as tabs and panels, ShinyCOPASI facilitates seamless exploration and sharing of models, enabling users to easily embed the model interface in their own websites. This user-friendly platform aims to augment the capabilities of COPASI by providing a flexible and dynamic environment for simulating and analyzing biochemical networks.

Deep learning's widespread adoption in science and engineering stems from its versatile capabilities, yet many scientists unfamiliar with its fundamentals overlook key considerations such as data regularization, optimization, overfitting, and feature selection. This textbook-style research paper focuses on the concept of uncertainty being actively applied in various fields to improve ML models and their experimental predictions. A comprehensive review of current methods for quantifying uncertainty in DNNs is provided, alongside a comparative analysis of these methods in the context of experimental data for a single parameter, as well as multiple parameters. The findings suggest that certain techniques outperform others across multiple performance metrics and domains, and our code has been made publicly available to facilitate replicability.

We compute the continuous tensor product of bimodules formed by central functions of a compact quantum group with itself. The resulting von Neumann algebra is shown to be a maximal abundance algebra, containing abundant copies of the basic quantum group's universal quantum group algebra. This study reveals that the basic quantum group's unitary quantum group U_q(g) has a von Neumann algebra with abundant copies of the free quantum group's standard quantum group algebra Z(q)(out)U_q(g).

Policy iteration comes with computational drawbacks in high-dimensional spaces. We have modified the algorithm to make it more efficient by incorporating an approximation step, which utilizes the GMRES method. The modified algorithm generates an approximate policy at each step and uses this approximation in the subsequent iteration. We introduce an error bound for the approximations, which enables us to control the total error and ensure the stability of the algorithm. We have tested the algorithm on various 3D and 2D maps and found that it offers significant reductions in computational time while maintaining accurate solutions when the tolerances are relaxed.

Let $G$ be a weighted directed graph, and consider the edge ideal $I(G)$, which is generated by oriented edges. This paper makes two primary contributions. First, it establishes a Hilbert-Samuel ring for $I(G)$ when $G$ has a specified property. Secondly, within the context of symbolic powers of $I(G)$, it identifies both a limit and whether this limit is strictly greater than zero.

To address inverse problems in complex computer simulations that produce large time series outputs, we develop a novel approach to model parameter identification. By reformulating the problem as a multi-dimensional optimization issue and employing a straightforward, efficient algorithm called contour, we overcome the challenges posed by large-dimensional spaces. Our time-series estimation method allows for simultaneous optimization of multiple parameters, leveraging their natural correlations. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach using hydrology-based computer simulations, showcasing its ability to accurately determine relevant parameters. Furthermore, we highlight that our method can successfully handle scenarios with limited flexible data and rapidly handle large-dimensional problems.

Robust learning algorithms are designed to operate effectively even when the training data is imperfect, potentially containing malicious inputs. A reliable approach for achieving robustness involves verifying the robustness of models using local inquiry, which involves examining the difference between the model's output and the label, even when the input has been slightly altered. Researchers have demonstrated that models trained using this method can operate reliably in the presence of malicious inputs. We investigate the conditions under which local inquiry proves useful for robust learning. Under certain circumstances, we find that it is possible to develop robust models without being exposed to malicious inputs at all. However, when the number of malicious inputs surpasses the number of harmless ones, we find that local inquiry proves ineffective. Fortunately, we also identify a range of parameters where it is possible to achieve robustness cost-effectively. Through our experiments, we verify that our theoretical findings align with practical reality.

For the first time, researchers have discovered that jet fragmentation changes in heavy Pb+Pb collisions at the LHC differ from those found in light proton-proton collisions. They used 5.02 TeV data from the CMS experiment, focusing on collisions where a high-energy photon had been recorded. By selecting beams with the same energy, they found that Pb+Pb collisions have a higher ratio of low-mass to high-mass hadron pairs within the jets, indicating that the collision medium affects the final particles. Notably, the team observed two breaks in the jet fragmentation function at approximately 0.2 and 0.5 TeV, and the former appeared sooner in Pb+Pb collisions than in proton-proton collisions.

Recent research involving Feynman integrals has highlighted the significance of Apéry-type inverse binomial series. Building upon previous findings that non-alternating central binomial series could be solved using the Shen-Liu method, we now show that alternating versions require a distinct approach due to their relationship with colored multiple zeta functions. Specifically, we demonstrate how alternating central binomial series can be evaluated when the sum of the fractions' denominators is an even multiple of 4, covering scenarios not covered in the initial Shen-Liu paper.

In 2020, the discovery of WISEA J153429.75-104303.3 was announced during the 49th meeting of the American Astronomical Society's Division on Planetary Sciences. Despite being named "The Mishap," this intriguing object remains an unsolved riddle. A recent photometric survey by the Zwicky Transient Facility has yielded significant data on the brown dwarf's activity. The existing data set contains six years of observations from the u and g bands, and 16 months of observations from the i and J bands. The brown dwarf's brightness displayed irregular u and g band patterns, while the I and J band observations showed consistent findings. The brown dwarf's general trend is noticeable in all bands, except for the u band due to its longer periods of brightness fluctuations. The study's long-term data have enabled researchers to determine the brown dwarf's spectral type and cloud coverage. Notably, the object's activity is notable but not exceptional compared to its peers. The discrepancy between the I and J band counts is thought to be the result of the brown dwarf's irregular cloud patterns. The brown dwarf's slow rotation period is consistent with high-level cloud coverage. The long-term data by the ZTF have allowed researchers to study the brown dwarf's activity cycles and potentially detect the onset of a new cycle.

The subatomic particles created in Xe-Xe high-energy collisions have been successfully reproduced by a theoretical framework that was initially applied to Pb-Pb interactions. Using the LHC's estimated collision conditions, a reliable account of how subatomic particles are formed is provided, encompassing rapid expansion and cooling of the colliding system. Our results are further supplemented by a comprehensive statistical analysis that enables direct comparison with official LHC experiments. Notably, our research successfully predicts the observed yields of long-lived particles short-handed as 'Hiroshima particles,' which are produced abundantly in the final stages of the high-energy collisions and then detected and analyzed by experimenters.

I will demonstrate how to apply and extend the concept of effective evolution to parton distribution functions at various scales, beginning with a basic explanation of the phenomenon in a physical system. Then, I will examine PDFs at two different scales, starting with a lower-scale PDF that is closely tied to a collective state with a short-lived nature and can be accurately described by a perturbative QCD calculation. This initial PDF can be evolved to a higher scale through an effective approach, incorporating both perturbative and non-perturbative components. To achieve this, I will utilize a framework combining instanton physics and PDF evolution, while also exploring an alternative approach based on the concept of effective actions. A key aspect of this method is that it enables the incorporation of instanton-induced effects up to any desired order of $e^{-\frac{2}{3}}$.

Specimens made of Martian and Lunar soil substitutes, in the form of cylinders, were created using press-molded technology and fired at various temperatures to examine how different temperatures affect their structure and strength. The experimental firing temperatures ranged between 900°C and 1400°C, allowing for the investigation of how temperature impacts the growth of pores and grain size in these materials. X-ray computed tomography was used to analyze the internal structure of the specimens, while compressive strength tests were conducted to evaluate their mechanical properties. The results showed that firing temperatures significantly affected both the microstructure and strength of the specimens, with optimal strength achieved at temperatures consistent with traditional ceramics, between 1200°C and 1300°C. These findings suggest that press-molded technology can be an effective base for creating structural ceramics in space, providing a valuable foundation for further development of 3D printing techniques to manufacture materials with controlled microstructures.

The dynamics of a liquid layer on a fiber influence the liquid's behavior when the fiber is withdrawn, impacting the formation of droplets. By numerically solving the Navier-Stokes equations for incompressible fluids, we analyzed the effects of liquid-surface tension and liquid-solid interaction. Our results show that high enough speeds when withdrawing the fiber can cause the liquid layer to slip, resulting in larger droplet diameters. Additionally, we discovered that lower liquid-solid interaction strengthens this phenomenon, while increased liquid-surface tension has an opposite effect on droplet production. Our study offers an explanation for the observed slip-induced enhancement in droplet formation.

A comprehensive measurement of the rate of new star formation within a galaxy can be achieved by analyzing the strength of a specific spectral line. However, predicting star formation rates using dust emission is challenging due to the intricate relationship between dust and stars. By comparing observed spectral data with simulated radiation patterns for different models, researchers can determine how much stars in a galaxy are emitting, although this estimation is prone to significant errors. By utilizing the strength of a bracket gamma line from 2masses survey and ages from PACS observations of nearby galaxies, we found that ages derived from SED fitting are too high by about 0.5 decades when the predicted rates are lower than approximately 5 solar masses per year, but the estimates become too low by about 0.25 decades when the predicted rates are higher than approximately 10 solar masses per year. We found that the discrepancy is likely due to the incomplete coral region of the dust, which affects the predicted rates more significantly for galaxies with lower star formation rates. Furthermore, we found a notable 0.2 dex difference in the predicted rates of nearby versus distant galaxies, which we found to be fully accounted for by the variation in the predicted dust absorption at 1 micrometers, indicating that lower star formation rates in distant galaxies result in a lower dust emission as the primary factor driving the predicted rates.

A significant area of study within quantum groups focuses on the nature of type II subgroups of the dual weight representations of the general linear Lie algebra.  We delve into this subject by examining a specific category of quantum subgroups associated with a finite group that appears in the fusion of the principal type II quantum subgroup of the group $GL_N\) and its dual.  By defining a new category of regions called $R_{\Pi}\mathcal{V}$ for any type II subgroup $\Pi$ of $GL_N$, we explore the structure of the regions and its relationship with the fusion of the subgroup and the characteristics of its dual weight representations.  The construction of the regional modules in $R_{\Pi}\mathcal{V}$ allows us to identify common structures among the dual weight representations of the subgroups for various choices of $\Pi$.  As a result, we establish a connection between the category of regions and the intersection rings of the Lusztig and Kashiwara-Tang small quantum groups $SL_qN$ and $SL_{q^2}N$.  The region corresponding to the dual weight representation in $R_{\Pi}\mathcal{V}$ is isomorphic to the subring of $SL_qN$ generated by the Lusztig integral forms of the root elements whose labels lie in a specific two-dimensional sector. This work addresses the general diffusion equation, incorporating both its linear and nonlinear variants. The paper proposes a novel method for solving this equation, which adapts the Lanchester equations from warfare dynamics. The approach is demonstrated on several examples, including the second-order differential equation, the modified mean-field equation, and the M-Mathieu equation. The method's utility in finding exact solutions for the general diffusion equation is illustrated.

This work addresses the task of recognizing handwritten mathematical expressions
from multi-touch device data. Each touch event is represented as a complex number,
encoding x and y coordinates, which are then transformed into polynomial series.
This transformation enables the conversion of touch data into a distinguishable
symbol-based feature. An FNN network was designed to process this feature and
generate a final output. Additionally, a touch prediction layer has been included
to foresee future touch inputs. An utter touch input represents a multi-touch event
and can be predicted with an anticipated touch part appended to the existing feature.
This anticipated touch part enhances the expression's structural information.
A multi-layer perceptron was trained to validate the effectiveness of the proposed
feature representation on a dataset of mathematical expressions. The results showed
a 50% increase in accuracy when the proposed feature and touch prediction layer
were used compared to the current standard method.

This paper introduces an innovative method for generating the duration information of synthetic speech by leveraging a median-based approach. Current duration modeling techniques often draw on statistical reasoning, yet this solution employs a non-parametric strategy. The novel duration model is integrated with a previously developed neural network-based speech synthesis system to create a comprehensive synthesis system. Evaluations of the new duration model suggest that it surpasses the performance of the original system, achieved through statistical duration modeling.

Species distribution analysis involves understanding the presence or abundance of species across various locations, which is essential in ecological research, conservation efforts, and management decisions. Researchers often use spatial models for species distribution analysis to account for correlations within data and diverse species characteristics. Theoretical models have limitations due to computational intensity and simplicity in handling multi-species cases. Bayesian inference provides an excellent alternative, offering a comprehensive framework for data analysis and interpretation. We introduced the spOccupancyR package, which offers a versatile solution for single, multiple species, and combined presences-absences data in a spatial context. The package utilizes Markov Chain Monte Carlo simulations to generate samples from the posterior distribution of interest, providing a comprehensive range of quantities and their associated uncertainties. We illustrate the spOccupancyR package through real-world case studies examining the distribution of two bat species and a combined analysis of ten species, which highlights its ability to handle complex data sets while maintaining ease of use and high computational efficiency.

This technical report outlines the advancements of the Skincare project, which has been detailed in a series of previous papers. The Skincare initiative is focused on developing an interactive decision support system for identifying and classifying skin cancers. By combining data from multiple sources, the team has created a decision support system consisting of a patient database, diagnostic algorithms, and classification tools. The decision support system utilizes interactive image processing techniques powered by artificial neural networks to aid dermatologists in diagnosing difficult cases, particularly those involving uncertain diagnoses or complex skin lesion interpretations.

To capture the intrinsic variability of Type Ia supernovae from limited spectral data, we developed a probabilistic autoencoder that preserves dimensionality of the data, rather than simplifying it. The model's generative process, guided by noise vectors, is visible through its latent space and predictive capabilities. The latent space demonstrates potential for differentiating unusual SNe Ia, while the model's generative noise exhibits variability comparable to the intrinsic luminosity variability of SNe Ia. However, our results indicate the model is insufficient for accurately distinguishing sub-classes of SNe Ia using spectral data alone. Future research could integrate the model with other supernova parameters for improved classification.

A massive neutral gas outflow has been detected in a young galaxy at a high rate of speed. The galaxy, named ofidie2217, is seen at a distance of approximately 8.7 kpc from the galaxy's centre at a redshift of 2.09. The outflow is revealed through the analysis of ALMA observations at a relatively low resolution. The data show a large neutral gas outflow with a significant extent of 1.9 kpc and an estimated mass flow rate of 500 $M_{\odot}$ per year. The outflow is likely driven by a system of star-forming regions at a high velocity of 500-600 km/s. The detection of this large neutral gas outflow suggests that a significant amount of gas is being expelled from the galaxy, which could affect the galaxy's star formation potential. The mass of the galaxy's stellar mass has been estimated at around 1.8*10$^{10}$ $M_{\odot}$. The galaxy's continued loss of gas could impact its potential to develop into a massive galaxy at a later time.

To study the movement of fluid into a column of lower density surrounded by a denser environment, we've developed a mathematical model. The fluid enters the column at a certain rate and encounters particles, which affects the flow's behavior as they accumulate at the base of the column. The resulting movement can be divided into distinct phases - an initial acceleration phase, a steady-state regime, and a phase characterized by large convective vortices. The model reveals that, unlike pure fluid dynamics scenarios, the onset of large convective vortices occurs earlier when particles are present. The study provides a framework for developing future theoretical models, and the predicted steady-state velocities match those observed in corresponding experiments.

Understanding how epidemics spread within a population, and ultimately die out, is a crucial area of study in the field of mathematical epidemiology. Although the analysis of epidemic models on graph theory has been extensively conducted, this research explores the application of hypergraphs to represent close contact interactions. By modeling the population as a hypergraph and deriving a general framework for analyzing epidemic models, this study obtains threshold criteria for the onset and disappearance of epidemics. Additionally, this approach enables the derivation of limiting parameters for the widely used Mean-Field approximation, improving upon its accuracy under certain conditions.

Recent breakthroughs in studying 2D magnetic structures have been highlighted by the discovery of effective spin laws in ultra-thin materials. In this research, effective spin laws are investigated in a CrI3 bilayer that exhibits a ferromagnetic properties. By applying the spin Hall machine technique to study electrical resistance in response to spin-orbit torques, we identified distinct responses related to the conservation of angular momentum in counter-rotating modes. Analysis using a magnetic layer model revealed two possible magnetic structures that originate from opposing magnetic layers with circular spin structures that oppose each other. One of these magnetic structure assumptions yields a Rashba-like effect at the interface, whereas both assumptions yield a chirality-related effect. By analyzing the effects of spin-orbit coupling and angular momentum conservation, we found that electrical resistance responses can be distinguished not only by their magnitude but also by their direction, paving the way for more intricate control of electrical resistance in 2D magnetic materials.

Previous studies on simulated solar-type dynamos have typically assumed solar rotation characteristics for their heliospheric applications. However, observations reveal that the Sun's rotation speed in the equatorial plane changes throughout the year due to its differential rotation, contrasting with the commonly used uniform rotation speed assumption. Notably, there are theories suggesting that the Sun's rotation rate might be slower in the equatorial regions, an anti-solar rotation pattern, which has yet to be explored in detailed numerical simulations. We conducted a study of global convection with a conserved angular momentum approach to investigate how various rotation parameters affect a solar-type dynamo. Our results demonstrate that when using the traditional solar rotation rate in a kinematic dynamo model, we obtain a weak and irregular magnetic cycle in the simulated Sun. In contrast, by utilizing an anti-solar rotation profile in the same dynamo model, we found a more pronounced and regular magnetic cycle, which may lead to the occurrence of magnetic cycles in slowly rotating stars.

Recent advancements in Deep Multimodal Learning have led to the development of methods handling K-fan out-of-vocabulary words in various applications such as natural language processing and image classification. Methods have been suggested to process multiple input modalities at once, but they typically do not have a shared understanding across inputs. This paper proposes a new general framework for a deep multimodal learning task with K-fan unknown words. The proposed framework uses a shared representation for learning modalities of the same type and can be easily adapted for applications involving multiple input modalities. Furthermore, we test this new framework on two specific tasks: multimodal image classification and word sense disambiguation. Our results indicate that the proposed framework performs better when compared to models without a shared representation.

McMini is a modern model verifier designed to validate the correctness of multithreaded C programs. McMini is an iterative model checker that employs DPOR, an advanced operational model, to efficiently handle complex inter-thread data dependencies. By recognizing that threads often follow predetermined patterns, McMini optimizes its operational model to incorporate pre-defined strategies for common thread paradigms, such as locks with queues. This strategic operational model leverages program-specific verification data to streamline the validation process. As a versatile tool, McMini comes bundled with a McMini-C compiler and a rich set of verification strategies that can be tailored to fit the needs of both basic and advanced model checking techniques.

The globally predominant messaging app, WhatsApp, has been criticized for allowing free dissemination of information, including misleading statements and fabricated news stories. To combat the spread of false information, WhatsApp introduced an experiment in India, allowing users to select groups to post fewer messages. In our study, we examine the effectiveness of this intervention by analyzing public opinion surveys conducted in India, focusing on misinformation-related attitudes among the survey's respondents. Our analysis reveals that non-forwarding users are more likely to hold WhatsApp responsible for combating misinformation, but our results show no significant shift in attitudes among all respondents. Therefore, we conclude that limiting message forwarding does not effectively alter public attitudes on combating misinformation.

We analyze a general branching population where individual lifetimes are independent and identically distributed with arbitrary distributions, and individuals give birth to new ones at random times following a Poisson process independently from their predecessors. It's assumed that the average time it takes for an individual to produce offspring is less than half the average time they remain alive, resulting in finite variance for both variables. It's further assumed that offspring numbers follow a distribution with finite variance and a specific form. It's found that long-term allele frequency distributions can be accurately represented by approximation using a specific method under these conditions, and numerical examples are provided to demonstrate the method's effectiveness. The method's performance is enhanced by incorporating simulation data for scenarios not covered by the provided theorems.

The primary goal of our spoofing countermeasure system is to identify artificial effects within spoken input that arise from speech synthesis or voice alteration techniques. We achieve this goal by incorporating a novel, attentive activation mechanism in our end-to-end system. This innovative approach enables our system to prioritize input features that we suspect have been artificially manipulated, ultimately leading to improved countermeasure performance. We tested various scenarios and found that our proposed system consistently outperforms conventional countermeasure systems. Notably, when counterfeiting attempts are particularly sophisticated and cover the entirety of spoken input, our solution excelled at distinguishing artificial effects, surpassing the performance of leading commercial systems.

Supergravity and 4-D string theory, which incorporate supersymmetry, typically require a high level of inflation to solve the cosmological problems and reset the universe conditions. Using a Goldstone boson-based approach, we have established a framework to analyze the properties of these supersymmetric inflationary models during the inflationary period. By applying a gradient expansion within the effective field theory of inflation, we have formulated a set of cosmological scaling conditions that maintain the model's validity. By examining the scaling behavior of heavy fields, we have reevaluated the Leptogenesis mechanism and its compatibility with the low-energy supersymmetry. Our analysis enables a more detailed comparison of the scalar particle spectra in models based on linear and non-linear symmetries, including the $N=1$ supergravity models with a nilpotent prepotent.

The intensity of photon pairs generated through spontaneous parametric downconversion exhibits correlations that extend beyond traditional intensity autocorrelation functions. We have demonstrated a notable asymmetry in these correlations when using a narrow wavelength-matched detection system. By adjusting the detection wavelength and considering the photonic Hamiltonian, we have observed that the correlation function's direction and magnitude can be manipulated. Furthermore, this research has been extended to a scenario involving non-linear interferometry, where the asymmetry in correlations significantly impacts the interferometer's ability to determine the phase shift.

We have developed an method for scanning terahertz radiation and have applied it to investigate the coupling mechanisms within arrays of microwave resonators. By doing so, we obtained precise images of the electric field distribution around each resonator in the array. Our research revealed that the coupling strength between adjacent resonators is primarily determined by the distance between them and not by their position relative to each other. Furthermore, we observed that the design of the resonators' geometry played a crucial role in determining their performance. Our study has important implications for the development of advanced terahertz quantum processors and could also contribute to the development of innovative microwave-based quantum processors.
We demonstrate that the union of Borel sets in the real numbers is uncountable, yet constitutes the entire real line. This proof follows directly from a similar finding for open intervals.

In the 2000s, hedge funds experienced significant growth, with individual investors and pension funds flocking to the sector in search of high returns. Research suggested that hedge funds' high returns stemmed from sophisticated short-term trading tactics, rather than the long-term fundamental analysis methods employed by mutual funds. We examine whether these hedge fund tactics can be replicated in an agent-based model and whether these models disrupt the market equilibrium, potentially explaining the superior returns associated with active trading strategies. Our research reveals that when all investors utilize the same algorithm, active management benefits those who initiate trades first, resulting from higher order execution. Conversely, when investors' actions are randomized, the superior returns associated with active strategies diminish, suggesting that hedge funds' high returns may be the result of a combination of favorable market conditions and the serial execution of trades by later actors.

A significant shift towards dynamic protocol detection in network traffic analysis has been observed in recent years, enabled by cutting-edge deep learning methods. This trend is particularly evident in open source network traffic analysis tools, where deep learning-based approaches have significantly improved accuracy. However, the use of deep learning in network traffic analysis is a relatively new concept, and the robustness of deep learning-based protocol detection models has yet to be thoroughly evaluated. This research assesses the effectiveness of open source network traffic analysis tools on detecting various network protocols in different traffic patterns. Specifically, it examines the ability of DeepFlow and Bro with deep learning-based classifiers to identify HTTP, DNS, and FTP protocols in diverse traffic scenarios. The results of this study reveal that these tools are susceptible to deep learning-based classifiers being confused by traffic resembling protocol non-traffic patterns, which can lead to inaccurate protocol detection. Furthermore, the results indicate that deep learning-based classifiers are vulnerable to traffic generated by low-quality protocols, which can also result in incorrect detection. This research provides new insights into the robustness of open source network traffic analysis tools, and its findings have significant implications for the deployment of deep learning-based protocol detection in real-world network traffic analysis applications.

Electrostatic gating limits the flow of electrons in integrated circuits. Another potential means of information transport, magnons derived from spin waves in magnetic materials, is difficult to regulate through electristatics. However, we found that superconducting strips atop thin magnetic films can completely attenuate magnons across a range of frequencies by producing localized magnetic fields that closely match the frequency of the magnons. By employing a formalism combining Usadel and semi-classical equations, we analyzed how a superconducting strip influences the nearby magnetic film and found that the resulting effect cannot be achieved through the existing means of magnon gating. The proposed method could be utilized to develop novel, quantum-enabled devices such as magnon transmitters and receivers.

A beneficial approach for gathering user insights while safeguarding user anonymity exists in federated learning. Nonetheless, novel classes emerge due to changes in user behavior or when transitioning to new tasks, necessitating updates to the classification model. There is still a need for a FL framework that can efficiently utilize data from diverse sources and accommodate emerging classes without necessitating an exhaustive data exchange. Our proposed framework addresses this challenge by allowing a classification model to generalize both existing and new classes without requiring data sharing. The framework's effectiveness is showcased through audio classification experiments on two intricate datasets, resulting in a notable enhancement of classification accuracy and a substantial reduction in communication required to adapt to the emerging classes.

A high-dimensional quantum system has the potential to overcome fundamental limitations in quantum communication. Topological features in high-dimensional entanglement can be explored using the multiqubit Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger state, which we examine in this context. We develop a measurement approach for the high-dimensional GHZ state and propose a method for detecting high-dimensional entanglement using the Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen correlation function. Our proposed measurement technique involves sampling pixels from a higher-dimensional image, which can be applied to entanglement-based quantum communication protocols to verify the security of secret keys. We discuss how this method can be adapted for use with noisy high-dimensional states, which are typically produced in experiments.

This research paper explores the problem of uplink cascade channel estimation in multi-user multiple-input-single-output systems enhanced by intelligent-reflecting-surfaces. To minimize the cost of estimating the complex surface and multi-user downlink-uplink channel, an optimized surface reflection scheme is developed, reducing channel estimation complexity and requiring fewer training signals. An efficient algorithm is proposed, using the surface's minimal pilot signals to accurately estimate the surface and users' channels, based on the surface's optimal training and the users' optimal detection. An iterative algorithm is developed, using the estimated surface and users' channels to refine the surface's reflection, based on the users' channels. An analytical study and simulations confirm the proposed solution's efficiency and resilience to uncertainties in the surface's reflection.

This study explores how COVID coverage by U.S. local news outlets relates to COVID deaths, cases, and the audiences of these news outlets, also considering the impact of news source type and state governance policies. Utilizing data from a content analytics service covering 450 U.S. news sources from January 2020 to June 2021, we calculated the frequency and seriousness of COVID-related news coverage for each state and ranked local news sources nationally based on these metrics. Combining the resulting data with public COVID statistics and governance policy information, we performed analyses at both state and local levels to reveal significant associations between COVID news coverage and deaths, cases, and policy changes. Additionally, we examined how COVID coverage varied among different news source types and populations affected by the pandemic. Our key findings include the correlation between local news COVID coverage and both deaths and cases, the distinction in COVID news coverage among locals, nationals, and public outlets, the connection between news coverage and government policy, and the influence of news source type on COVID coverage.

We developed a neuroscientific model to study the cognitive progress of counting in non-human primates. This model combines a simplified version of the theoretical framework for the hierarchical representation of numbers in the brain, with the reinforcement learning mechanism for complex decision-making processes. We utilized a memory-augmented recurrent neural network to simulate the complex temporal dynamics of these interactions. By training this model and analyzing its results, we identified key factors that influence learning progress in counting. Our findings indicate that a specific region of the brain, specifically the medial intraparietal sulcus, plays a crucial role in mastering numerical tasks.

Bloom filters provide efficient solutions to situations involving large amounts of data, including approximate matching and data compression. While they offer a good compromise between speed and accuracy, they often require more space than needed for their intended purpose. To address this, alternative filters like Morton filters and Cuckoo filters have been developed. However, all existing solutions fall short in at least one aspect – either they require excessive space or an unacceptable level of false positive errors. To mitigate this, a new type of filter called Xor Filter has been introduced, which combines elements from compact and high-performance designs. By incorporating two changes – using 8-bit hash values and utilizing bit strings of any length – the Xor Filter surpasses the performance capabilities of both Morton and Cuckoo filters, while also achieving superior compactness rates. In particular, the new filter can reach speeds similar to high-performance designs (like Bloom and Cuckoo filters) while reducing space requirements by approximately two times. To achieve this level of improvement, a novel approach to designing efficient Bloom filters is introduced, which incorporates key elements from the Xor Filter design.

This brief note outlines a correspondence between convex geometry and complex Autodiff manifolds, demonstrating equivalent relationships between certain convex properties and their counterparts in K\"ahler-Einstein geometry with potential $c_1(M) \leq 0$. Specifically, key convex properties in Euclidean, hyperbolic, and spherical spaces have direct translations to distinct classes of smooth Finsler metrics, further illustrating connections to the moduli spaces of binary dustions.

A new approach to market analysis is proposed, utilizing a sequence of transaction prices, executed at respective time points, to develop predictive indicators of predictive indicators, thereby creating a hierarchy of predictive indicators. This process involves incorporating future transaction data, albeit in a non-causal and abstracted form. It enables the derivation of indicators unaffected by real-time noise, as future prices are incorporated into the analysis. To achieve this, a sequential testing method is employed to identify significant price trends among various time intervals, using statistical distributions tailored to the structure of transaction data. By ascending the hierarchy of predictive indicators, a series of predictive indicators are developed, refining our understanding of market dynamics and opening new avenues for research.

This work presents FLVoogd, a refined federated learning framework, designed to address potential data collisions and guarantee participant privacy. In FLVoogd, a secure hardware environment and virtualised client structures enable the creation of secure and trusted interfaces for data processing and communication. By integrating the hardware-intrinsic security capabilities of Voogd and a provenised, FLVoogd offers robust protection against malicious and untrusted clients, as well as internal threats. Using FLVoogd, experiments were conducted with MNIST and CIFAR10 datasets to test the effects of data collisions and privacy breaches. These experiments demonstrated the efficiency and privacy security capabilities of FLVoogd in complex federated learning environments.

We successfully completed the winning solution to the NeurIPS 2021 - AWS DeepDrive autonomous driving challenge using a task pipeline of object detection, trajectory planning, and control adjustment. Our approach integrated an image-based method for predicting the leader vehicle's future trajectory, allowing the system to adapt to the unpredictability of the leader's movement. By incorporating gradient information from real-world images into the network and utilizing a multi-task training process, we achieved superior results on real-world driving scenarios, thereby addressing the significant gap between simulated and real-world performances. Our challenge submission video is available at https://youtu.be/pOverG4kU6I.

Deepfake creation techniques, particularly image and video generation using deep learning algorithms, have become increasingly powerful. Researchers have developed new methods such as OGI deepfake denouncer and DeepNude-like algorithms, which can create deepfakes quickly. However, the current state of deepfake detection is largely fragmented and research is necessary to achieve reliable results. This study introduces a comprehensive solution, starting by presenting a new dataset comprising high-quality videos with adjustable DeepNude-generated patches. The proposed dataset is accompanied by a novel method that integrates patch-based deepfake detection, enabling more effective identification of deepfake videos. The research includes an analysis of various deepfake creation and detection methods and showcases the efficacy of human-made deepfake videos.

The equilibrium between various chemical states in a planet's core and mantle affects its core heat budget and, in turn, its magnetic field strength and potential magnetic environment. A comprehensive re-examination of the Fe$^{3+}$-H$^{+}$-SiO$_2$ model for sub-Neptune GJ 1215 b reveals transit signatures that correspond to a liquid water layer at or above the pressure required for water to dissolve Fe$^{3+}$ ions. This layer can produce notable transit dimming associated with the core heat due to differences in opacity across various temperature states. Core entropy can also be determined by the boundary layer's thermal gradient, which in turn depends on the mantle's thermal radius relative to the planet's radius. Observations of these signatures in the near-infrared can be used to measure the radius of a water layer or the radius of the planet's core, or to identify the presence of an atmosphere overlaying a liquid water layer. Furthermore, observations in the green and red can be used to measure the radius of a water layer or the radius of the planet's core, or to identify the presence of an atmosphere overlaying a liquid water layer. Notably, a thorough re-examination of the 3D model for GJ 1215 b reveals that the core entropy estimated in 2019 is associated with the core heat due to a liquid water layer at or above the pressure required for water to dissolve Fe$^{3+}$ ions.

Inspired by diverse biological systems, the synapse-dependent plasticity rule can learn complex patterns in spiking neural networks through a gradient-free process. Our study focuses on two primary aspects of this rule: how it chooses the optimal weight for connections and its dependence on local properties of networks. We have engineered a novel form of the rule that learns weights in a manner consistent with biological principles, is efficient to compute, and is applicable to large complex networks. Our model's performance has been tested with datasets including the MNIST dataset, resulting in results comparable to those achieved with more sophisticated methods. Additionally, the networks trained with our algorithm exhibit synapse-specific weight distribution patterns and group size effects similar to those observed in biological systems.

This document outlines the key challenges and requirements for the out-of-category challenge as part of the 2022 NLP Transfer Learning for End-to-End Navigated Dialogue Workshop. 

The out-of-category challenge focuses on evaluating models' ability to adapt to new categories of data beyond what they were trained on, presenting this year in the form of two distinct tasks centered around ordering information in two different datasets. 

We outline the specific criteria and assessment methods for the out-of-category challenge, including uncontrolled and controlled conditions, as well as the metrics and evaluation processes used to determine the final model rankings. 

Ultimately, the out-of-category challenge serves as a call to action for the NLP community to drive innovation in out-of-category performance, with the goal of enhancing flexible and adaptable language models capable of navigating new categories of data effectively.

A specific type of generalized polynomial chaos expansion is verified in this study, specifically verifying its accuracy using the Kriging method. This verification focuses on post-hoc evaluation, meaning it assesses the errors after the computations have been completed. In contrast to traditional a priori analysis, which predicts the accuracy of methods before use, post-hoc evaluation analyzes the actual performance of methods. This approach enables the evaluation of several parameters that influence the results. Additionally, we propose an adaptive procedure for selecting the most effective parameters and evaluate the performance of polynomial chaos expansions with different levels of complexity.

We have developed and investigated an adaptive method for identifying and
recognizing changes in data streams. The proposed method acknowledges that in
many real-world scenarios, not all variables' historical data is available before
a change occurs. However, it can utilize pre-change data for any subset of the
variables and then adapt to changing conditions for all variables. Our goal is
to minimize the detection and isolation time while controlling the false alarm
rate. The performance of the proposed adaptive approach is evaluated under two
scenarios: when the distributions before and after a change are known, and when
only the latter is known. Established bounds show that the detection time
increases linearly on the number of variables and logarithmically on the number
of observations, while the isolation time is proportional to the number of
variables. When the distributions are unknown, empirical results indicate that
the detection time is nearly linear on the number of variables and logarithmic
on the number of observations. The method's performance is compared to ideal
benchmarks, including one that utilizes complete historical data and another that
has prior knowledge of the change point.

We have obtained spectroscopic data for 54 dwarf galaxies between 0.0004 and 0.0398 redshift, which we analyzed using multiple techniques to understand their composition and star formation history. Our research shows that systems with high metal content experience more gradual and less intense periods of star formation compared to low-metality galaxies. The times between initial formation and peak star formation range from 1.6 (+/-0.9) billion years for low-metality galaxies to 6.6 (+/-1.2) billion years for high-metality galaxies. However, we found no correlation between metal content and galaxy brightness. By examining alpha-element ratios, we discovered that galaxies with low metal content exhibit greater suppression of these elements, indicating shorter formation times. Furthermore, we compared our findings to a hydrodynamic simulation, revealing that galaxies with low metal content resemble the simulation's initial stages, whereas high-metality galaxies resemble the simulation's later stages with established active star formation.

Given a profinite group $\Gamma$, we define the homotopy action spectrum as an element in the spectrum of the non-connective profinite spectrum $\pi_{-*}\pi_{\pm*}(\mathbb{Z}[\Gamma])$ that supports $\Gamma$, which can be thought of as a way to incorporate the homotopy action of $\Gamma$ on a space $X$, defined when $\Gamma$ acts homotopically freely and finitely on $X$, by embedding it into the spectrum corresponding to the free profinite $\mathbb{Z}[\Gamma]$-module supplied with the profinite $\mathbb{Z}[\Gamma]$-action it inherits from the tensoring of $\pi_{\pm*}(\mathbb{Z}[\Gamma])$. A key finding is that the resulting spectrum $\hat{X}_{\Gamma}$ carries a natural action by $\Gamma$, which turns out to be an essential tool in establishing a homotopy-invariant expression for the profinite group's homotopy of unoriented linear maps applied to the spectrum $\hat{X}_{\Gamma}$.

Accurate extraction of useful information from diverse document types, such as receipts, IDs, and letters, is crucial in numerous real-world settings. However, manually labeling data for such applications is extremely time-consuming and often impractical due to the labor involved in examining physical documents. In many cases, businesses do not have the necessary personnel to devote time to labeling data. This challenge can be resolved through the use of semi-supervised learning, a deep learning technique that reduces the cost of data labeling. By taking both labeled and unlabeled data into account, semi-supervised learning models can be trained to extract information from visually complex documents without breaking the budget. This innovative solution enables the automatic labeling of a large number of documents, streamlining the labeling process and making it more efficient for businesses to deploy extractive models in real-world settings.

The interface electronic properties of the EuS/InAs heterostructure have been studied using a quantum-chemical model and different computational tools to analyze the behavior of the spin-polarized 4f electrons of europium. Two possible arrangements of the EuS/InAs interface were examined: one where indium atoms from the InAs crystal position themselves directly above the europium atoms from the EuS crystal (ideal configuration), and another where the InAs crystal is slightly shifted relative to the EuS crystal (misaligned configuration). Our analysis revealed notable differences in the electronic structures of these two configurations and showed that the 4f electron cloud of europium in the misaligned configuration is more strongly interacting with the indium atoms from the InAs crystal compared to the ideal configuration. Additionally, our results from our calculations aligned with experimental evidence showing a particular spectral shift in the EuS/InAs interface. Our analysis also highlighted how the spin-polarized 4f electron cloud of europium in the misaligned configuration forms strong bonds with the p-like orbitals of adjacent indium atoms from the InAs crystal.

A fundamental concept in mathematical logic, the Baire space $\omega^\omega$ supports a rich hierarchy of Borel sets, with the Wadge degrees serving as the primary framework for categorizing these sets based on their decision-making capabilities. The Wadge degrees are defined through an comparison process involving continuous bisisomorphic relations, with higher degrees indicating more efficient decision-making capabilities. The classification system consists of $\bot$ (undecidable), $[]$ (uncomputable but computably bounded), and several levels of capability up to $[]^\omega$. Our investigation adds four new levels to this system: $\ []_{\Pi^0_n}$ for $n\geq\omega$ and $\ []_{\Sigma^0_n}$ for $0\leq n\geq\omega$. The primary challenge in this research is to demonstrate that the new classes do not fall under the existing categories of $\ []_{\Pi^0_n}$ or $\ []_{\Sigma^0_n}$ for $0\leq n\leq\omega$. The results show that the Borel Wadge degrees can be efficiently classified in a finite number of steps, with the complexity of classifications tied to the levels of $\ []_{\Pi^0_n}$ for $1\leq n\leq\omega$ and the structure of infinite trees.

Deep, wide, and complex Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are emerging as preferred models for real-world clicking tasks due to their ability to produce more accurate results; however, their high computational costs hinder their widespread adoption in mobile devices. Previous studies on pruning have focused on enhancing model inference efficiency, but their approaches often compromise both the model's accuracy and structural integrity. Consequently, the improved inference efficiency obtained through pruning cannot be fully leveraged in enhancing the model's training efficiency. Therefore, we propose ClickTrain, the first pruning-based approach tailored specifically for clicking tasks, which aims to efficiently train models via a precise and architecture-preserving pruning technique. ClickTrain's key components include (1) the ClickNet model, which uses the reparameterization trick to model click probabilities as a response to latent perceptions, and (2) the PruneNet tool, which employs a perception-level pruning strategy to remove unnecessary model parameters while maintaining the original model's structural accuracy. By leveraging the distributional information of click labels during pruning, ClickTrain can further optimize model sparsity to achieve significant training efficiency gains without compromising model precision or structural integrity, thereby enabling the development of accurate models directly from mobile devices. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of ClickTrain in achieving both precise model pruning and training, outperforming existing pruning methods.

This research examines the properties of modal operators within distributive complete Lambek calculus, specifically how they interact with the left and right fragmentation rule. We discover that employing the left rule is sufficient for obtaining all modal operator proofability invariants. Consequently, we have developed new and strengthened proof techniques for the Lambek calculus. Our findings also highlight the equivalency between right modalization and the left modalization by contrapositive. Additionally, we have identified an approach to generating modal multimodal connectives and have explored the duality between the Lambek calculus and its dual system.

The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have detected a full year of signals resulting from the coalescence of black hole and neutron star binary systems, providing substantial datasets for analysis. However, the vast space of possible observations poses significant computational challenges to optimal extraction methods. We have developed a deep convolutional neural network that can automatically identify signals from its inputs, similar to how the human visual system functions. Its performance surpasses traditional methods when the signal-to-noise ratio is lower than 20 and rival's performance matches optimal extraction methods for higher signal-to-noise ratios. Furthermore, our network demonstrates superior accuracy in classifying binary systems' components compared to a previous approach.

A new discovery has been made regarding a gas giant exoplanet, which orbits a host star called TOI-5542 approximately every 75 days. Initial analysis suggests the exoplanet, which has a radius similar to that of Jupiter, may actually be a larger warm Jupiter. Further investigation into the exoplanet's properties could reveal significant new insights into its characteristics and its formation and evolution processes, particularly given the host star's notably metal-poor composition in contrast to its relatively old age. TOI-5542 is an older star with an estimated age of approximately 8.5 billion years, which is deemed ancient on a cosmic scale. Moreover, the exoplanet's size and the distance between its orbit and the host star present an interesting case study for future studies focused on its potential physical changes over time.

Sequential decision-making in operations management problems, such as those governed by Constraints Markov Decision Processes (CMDPs), often require optimizing control policies that account for resource limitations and regulatory requirements. The resulting optimal policies, often referred to as the \emph{optimal} or \emph{efficient} policies, ensure that constraints are fully utilized and resources are managed effectively. The literature discusses two types of optimal policies - the first based on the Lagrangian approach and the second developed through the sampling-based method, both of which suffer from limitations. The sampling-based method, for example, has difficulties dealing with a large number of constraints while the Lagrangian approach has issues dealing with non-convex policies. To overcome these limitations, researchers have proposed alternative formulations and solving strategies. One such example is the application of the primal-dual subgradient method (PDSG) which has been successfully used in optimizing multi-objective MDPs and is now being evaluated in the context of CMDPs.

This research paper introduces an advanced method for recognizing handwritten mathematical equations offline. Unlike other approaches that depend on pen inputs, our technique extracts a single unified image of the equation from a sensor, enabling recognition through a single process. We utilize a unique symbol representation focused on key visual features and train a fully convolutional network to achieve exceptional recognition performance. Notably, our method demonstrates robust tolerance to noise and hand-written variations. Additionally, we incorporate an innovative equation rendering system, enabling two-handed pen-input interactions, where users can interact with recognized math through 3D printed objects. Furthermore, we showcase how our method facilitates a range of enhanced mathematical search capabilities on handwritten notes.

We find connections between the growth of cohomology dimensions in supersymmetric quantum mechanics and sheaf cohomology, exploring various scenarios such as dimension growth, stability, and simplicity. In complex dimension d, a simplified model reveals that cohomology grows exponentially in d+1 steps, while in a general framework, an indirect limit on cohomology dimensions exists. Additionally, certain supersymmetric quantum systems are linked to grassmann bundles and nilpotent cones, enabling the calculation of cohomology dimensions through the construction of explicit global sections under specified conditions.

By examining the link dynamics in a large network, researchers can gain insights into the inherent complexities of the system. Despite this, there isn't a universally accepted theory that can predict and explain fluctuations in network connectivity. These fluctuations, when analyzed, may reveal the system's potential for significant changes. This could entail switching to a more stable configuration or even collapse, which poses a significant risk to system stability. Consequently, understanding the variability of network interactions is essential for creating early warning systems to predict and mitigate potential disasters. Our study aims to address this challenge by investigating the relationship between network diameter and the diversity of interactions at different time scales in both growing networks and those obtained through the mean-field analysis of a dynamical model. Our findings suggest a general pattern, where the abundance of interactions increases as the system evolves over shorter time periods. Moreover, this research reveals a critical time point, $t_*$, where the abundance of interactions begins to decline and may serve as a potential warning sign for a system on the verge of a sudden change. To further explore this phenomenon, we also developed a test to assess the variability of network interactions and identified several factors that influence this complexity. Ultimately, our study provides a framework for discovering and characterizing variability in network interactions, which can be applied to a broad range of problems involving complex system dynamics.

Actor-critic reinforcement learning has significant applications in areas such as decision-making and control. The integration of the Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) method into actor-critic models has been proven to be highly effective. This work seeks to understand the reasons behind this success by examining the relationships between the HMC-induced gradients and the critical gradients in both the critic and actor networks. A novel lemma has been established to facilitate this analysis. By leveraging the HMC-induced gradients, a more efficient critic network can be optimized, leading to improved critical policy evaluations. Furthermore, the insights gained enable the development of an actor-critic method with adapted variance reduction, which enables bi-directional communication between the critic and actor networks, ultimately resulting in enhanced actor updates and actor-critic policy training. This method has been rigorously evaluated against existing benchmarks, achieving superior performance in a diverse range of reinforcement learning tasks.

Autonomous systems navigating complex environments with reduced visibility demands
strong sensory capabilities to avoid collisions. This paper focuses on implementing
a sensing system utilizing sonar technology for mobile robot navigation. To ensure
sensory data reliability, we introduce an adaptive sonar data processing technique,
sonar vectoring, to enhance sensing consistency and avoid interference. Our proposed
sonar data processing method is seamlessly integrated with a layered navigation controller
for optimal performance. Furthermore, we conduct extensive experimental testing on
an navigation controller system equipped with an mobile robot platform, aiming to
investigate the impact of sensory data adaptation on navigation error and system
stability.

NII Nereid, a small satellite of Neptune, has been studied using its
reflectance spectrum observed in 1993 via the Infrared Telescope Facility.
NII Nereid's surface is comprised of ice and rock mixtures that contain
water ice pure or frozen with various percentages of magnesium iron
silicates. Closely orbiting the Neptunian system, this satellite most
likely originated from Neptune's atmosphere. The presence of water ice
exposes NII Nereid's surface to space, which is protected from solar wind
by the satellite's thin atmosphere. Analyzing NII Nereid's composition in
detail is essential in understanding the processes on small bodies orbiting
Neptune-Centaur planets. The percentages of water ice in NII Nereid's
compositional models have been estimated to range from 20% to 100%. The
best fit models include surfaces made up of 70% water ice pure and frozen
with magnesium iron silicates to varying degrees. Although NII Nereid is
too small to have an differentiated interior, it is believed to have formed
in the same place as larger, icy bodies in the solar system. The percentages
