Let $\mathcal{R}_n(q)$ be the ring of lower triangular matrices of order $n \geq 2$, consisting of elements from the finite field $F(q)$ of order $q \geq 2$. Additionally, let $V_{2n}(q)$ be the free left module of its counterpart ${^2T_n(q)}(q)$, consisting of matrices with a specific rank. Studies have proven that both $(F(q), +)$ and ${^2T_n(q)}(q), \cdot)$ resemble affine planes, and further show that both have lines isomorphically related to projective lines of order $q$. More importantly, this paper finds that both structures are actually affine planes isomorphically related to either $F(q^2, +)$ or $F(q, +)$.

This research involves examining various model-theoretic properties on the Tukey-order with respect to powers of countable structures. We start by considering the completeness of these ordered sets. Then, in a step-down approach, we discuss the existence of most numerous classes, maximal chains, and maximal non-comparable substructures. Along the way, we compare these properties to foundational results established by Pawlikowski.

A new method is introduced for improving a policy's ability to increase a system's negative characteristics, specifically optimality and novelty in a setting with unobserved factors. This enhanced policy, driven by a dynamic treatment regime, is based on a Bayesian learning strategy that estimates its effects through data. Key aspects of this approach involve leveraging the counterfactual connections inherent in the Bayesian framework and incorporating uncertainty into the analysis. It employs a straightforward metric for evaluating counterfactual outcomes and relies on a simplified assumption about the treatment's impact structure. Simulation studies have demonstrated that this optimized policy yields greater optimality and novelty levels compared to the standard Bayesian treatment regime. Furthermore, the optimized regime exhibits more efficient characteristics in scenarios with limited additional data constraints.

Duality between abstract algebraic structures provides crucial insights into the properties of duality itself, enabling the construction of complete lattices from dualities on categories of topological spaces. This paper's first two sections examine the basic properties of dualities and their power in generating such lattices. Building on this foundation, the third section explores how certain criteria for homological theories imply the existence of dualities that can interpret those theories. Specifically, this implies the existence of dualities that can interpret theories such as Ab, Coherent cohomology, and Grothendieck cohomology when combined with additional assumptions. The final section applies these findings to homological theories associated with geometric categories.

A set of thirty distinct elements $\{\eta_I\}_{I=1}^{30}$ is created by taking a $E_8$ lattice and multiplying it by the square root of a prime number ($p$) and then dividing the results by unique divisors of $288$. The elements $\{\eta_I\}$ form the core of a larger system, with eight distinct elements $\{\eta_j\}_{j=1}^{8}$ constituting a reference system. By applying a quantum operator to the elements $\{\eta_I\}$ and computing the resulting projections onto both the $E_8$ lattice and a weight lattice based on a Cayley transform of $E_8$, the authors generate a range of entangled states and study their connections to nonlocality and contextuality. In particular, the authors examine six different configurations of entanglement, with two of these configurations serving as a starting point to explore the entanglement of ten distinct elements $\{\xi_k\}_{k=1}^{10}$.

A phenomenon known as topological superconductivity occurs when superconductors possess certain properties of symmetry that protect certain characteristics even when they are cut or damaged. Using a model of interacting electrons on a graph-based geometric structure, we demonstrate the emergence of topological superconductors in a specific type of superconducting material consisting of multiple bands. One of these bands is designed to mimic the characteristics of high-temperature superconductors made of iron, while another is based on a simple mathematical concept and serves as a normal conductor reference point. By adjusting a band's smoothness under physical constraints, we discover that the topological superconducting threshold is not only influenced by an underlying topological number but also varies according to how smooth the band is. This finding is substantiated numerically. Furthermore, we define a geometrically-based characteristic called the quantum smoothness of a band and propose it as an essential property of topological superconductivity.

The Gaussian distribution is uniquely determined by the distribution of a linear combination and a power function of independent identically distributed random variables. We identify the distributions of pairs of variables such that the one-dimensional subgroups of their respective groups exhibit this characteristic, thereby proving a generalized version of the theorem originally stated by Polya.

Presence-absence data is represented as binary vectors or sparse vectors with numerous zeros. These data points appear in high-dimensional spaces and are commonly found in fields like genomics, microarray analysis, and taxonomic research. Effective analysis of such data necessitates appropriate statistical methods that can accommodate the inherent sparsity. This study compares various clustering approaches suitable for sparse data in dimension reduction, density-based, hierarchical, and model-based categories. It employs simulated datasets based on the beta-binomial model to assess their performance under different sparsity levels and clustering configurations. Furthermore, the evaluation of clustering methods is challenged by the absence of true cluster information for real-world datasets. Consequently, this study utilizes predicted clustering structures and statistical measures such as the Adjusted Rand Index and the Variable Importance Metric in Random Forests to demonstrate the efficacy of these clustering methods on actual presence-absence datasets, including plant species data and human microbe data. The implementation of these techniques is available through the spclust package on CRAN and GitHub.

In the last few years, salient object detection using deep neural networks has gained significant attention due to their impressive performance. Notably, dealing with RGB and RGB-D images that contain spatial and depth information has proven to be a powerful approach to improve salient object detection accuracy. Most existing methods tackle these tasks separately, ignoring potential improvements. To address this, we propose an efficient and general framework that unifies RGB and RGB-D salient object detection, leveraging the inherent benefits of integrated spatial and depth information. Our framework consists of two components: a base network for spatial image salient object detection and a depth fusion module to incorporate depth information. Through comprehensive experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework, showcasing its superiority over existing approaches in terms of accuracy and efficiency. The proposed framework's source code and models can be found on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/Ai-Little-Umbrella/Deep-Attention-RGB-D.

This paper showcases our BERT and SVM-based approaches to Subtask A in SemEval-2019's Identifying Aggressive Texts challenge. Our results indicate that a BERT-based model trained on a single UK dataset yielded a F1 score of 0.5244, while an ensemble of SVMs from various text features achieved a 0.3146 F1 score. Notably, both scores fall short of the challenge's baseline. To enhance performance, we suggest combining rich text features with learning-based methods utilizing deeper neural networks like BERT.

A number n is defined as having palindromic quotients if it satisfies the condition that for every number d that divides n, the quotient n divided by d is also a palindrome. In this paper, a different definition is introduced, where a number n is considered to have palindromic quotients if there exists another number d such that n divided by d results in a palindrome. It is demonstrated that the numbers conforming to this new definition can be represented as the product of a number k and k plus 1, where both k and k plus 1 are prime numbers. Additionally, the paper explores the notion of non-palindromic quotients for numbers. A distinct case is examined where a number n has non-palindromic quotients based on a different definition, where the quotient n divided by d is not a palindrome. It is shown that this case corresponds to numbers n that are multiples of six, specifically those that satisfy the condition where d divides n minus n reversed, where n reversed is the reverse of n.

Computational tomography (CT) is widely utilized for detecting various materials within objects; however, its limitations are underscored when attempting to image multiple energies and various attenuators simultaneously. A novel non-convex framework aims to reconcile this challenge by balancing data fidelity and smooth variations across different parameters. Influenced by convex decomposition approaches, this framework incorporates distinct penalty terms for sensor noise, density, and label variations. Furthermore, a convex regularization term derived from polyenergetic beam hardening propagation principles (PHPP) is included to stabilize the solution and ensure consistency across distinct energies. By iteratively minimizing the non-convex energy with alternating minimization (ANM) algorithm, accurate reconstructions of image intensity, sensor noise, density, and material labels are obtained simultaneously. The proposed method is robust to sensor noise and sensitive to energy variations, as supported by both noise-free and noisy phantom and patient scans.

Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) is a complex task due to the complexity of handwritten texts and the diversity of writing systems. While significant progress has been achieved, HTR for less common languages and scripts remains a challenging area of study. This research focuses on developing a novel approach for HTR, which doesn't require extensive labeled data typically needed for training advanced neural network models. Composing word-level templates with sub-unit components is a key aspect of this proposed method. By leveraging the architecture of existing letter-level sequence-to-sequence models, this approach enables the direct generation of word-level sequences using learned phoneme, syllable, and consonant-vowel templates. Evaluation results indicate that this method produces word-level sequences with a significant portion of correct words, showcasing its potential as a data production technique for handwritten text recognition.

To merge results from ab initio methods for nuclei composed of different number of protons and neutrons, calculations require significant resources as the number of required basis functions rapidly grows with an increase in the nucleon mass. This work introduces three methods to merge calculations for stable nuclei and applies them to closed and open-shell nuclei, examining in detail the convergence of 4He, 40Ca, and 56Fe calculations. Then, merged calculations for 40Ca and 56Fe are used to formulate new estimates for their axial vector coupling constants g_A. This new technique surpasses existing calculations based on saturation hypothesis and is a crucial first step towards applying merged calculations to nuclei at the limits of stability.

Concepts in topological quantum phenomena have garnered significant interest from researchers in the quantum information and communication field due to their intrinsic properties and the potential for future applications. The SSH model serves as a fundamental starting point for educating newcomers to the field and introducing the concepts of topological quantum numbers. This review delves into various ideas associated with the SSH model starting with its initial development, and we examine various notions related to edge states, degeneracy, and topological characteristics. We also discuss the eigenvalue, entropy, and information-based indices that emerge in this context and explore the connections to topological properties. Finally, we review the various concepts of dynamical phenomena associated with the SSH model.

This study examines the compactness of composition operators within the Bergman spaces associated with certain planar domains and analytic circles in the $\mathbb{C}^2$. Specifically, consider a planar domain with its boundary sufficiently close to being smooth and convex, and let $B$ be a bounded Borel measure with its support in the domain or its boundary. Suppose $B$ meets specific mass conditions; define the Bergman kernel as $\eta_{\lambda}$ for the domain with its associated Bergman kernel bilinear form $B_{\lambda}$. If a continuous operator $C$ maps one Bergman space to another, and if there exists a sequence of operators $C_n$ that is uniformly bounded in norm and whose images are contained in the finite-dimensional subspace of $\lambda B_{\lambda}$, then the composition operator $C$ is compact. Similarly, this principle can be applied to analyze the compactness of other types of operators. Notably, sufficient conditions for compactness in this context are significantly weaker than those in existing literature. Additionally, this study investigates the compactness of other types of operators that have received less attention in existing literature. Specifically, it establishes compactness criteria for translation operators, operators induced by weighted Bergman projections, and operators induced by differentiation with respect to one variable. We derived the two-loop amplitude for five-dimensional supergravity in AdS$_5$ using a direct computational approach. We also developed an algorithm to convert this amplitude into a standard form via a Poincar\'e transformation. Furthermore, we verified that the converted amplitude is equivalent to the three-point vertex of $\mathcal{N}=1$ superconformal field theory defined on flat space. We then applied our method to calculate the two-loop supergravity amplitude on AdS$_5$ with an internal SYM partner, which corresponds to a four-point vertex in the SCFT. We observed that the amplitude can be decomposed into a baselined component and a nonvanishing transverse sector, occurring in SUSY cases only. We used our results to confirm that the Baseline + Transverse decomposition of the Amplitude = Flat Space Amplitude, a relationship previously hypothesized by prentice. We used our results to confirm that the Baseline + Transverse decomposition of the Amplitude = Flat Space Amplitude, a relationship previously hypothesized by Prentice.

High-performance computing on GPUs with massive parallel processing capabilities has been widely adopted across various fields, but programming them effectively proves challenging due to complex memory management requirements. The memory allocation process on GPUs is particularly complicated by constraints such as contiguous memory access, shared memory limitations, and block-level memory allocation. Existing memory allocators on GPUs struggle to cope with these constraints, leading to inefficiencies that can result in memory waste, fragmentations, and performance degradation. In an effort to improve memory utilization and maximize GPU memory capacity, a new dynamic memory allocator called DynaSOAr has been developed for object-based programming on GPUs. DynaSOAr features a parallel memory allocation approach that leverages a memory management arena to minimize fragmentation and optimize memory access through the use of a hash table. By employing arena memory management and incorporating a double-list data structure, DynaSOAr enables efficient and parallel memory allocation on GPUs, ultimately leading to significant gains in memory efficiency and throughput.

We introduce several $U(1)_X$ models derived from a high-scale $SO(10)$ gauge theory. The existing literature on these models lacks a comprehensive model-building framework, which our work aims to establish by incorporating two unique features. Firstly, we impose a $U(1)_Y$ charge assignment that maintains charge conjugation in three-generation fermions, while allowing the $U(1)_X$ charge can be fully determined by combining this constraint with existing grand unified theory (GUT) charge assignments. Secondly, we propose a new $U(1)_Y$ charge assignment that maintains charge conjugation in three-generation fermions, which our method allows. The proposed $U(1)_X$ models can address the SU(2)_L doublet-higgs scalar mass, either in the range of 10 TeV to 30 TeV or above 30 TeV, depending on the unknown $X$ mass. The scalar potential in these models is shown to be stable against unstable directions, with one case, however, requiring additional fine-tuning. We present a detailed analysis of particle spectrum, fermion Yukawa interactions, and gauge boson masses, along with an evaluation of $Z$-$X$ mixing in the $U(1)_Y$ and $U(1)_X$ gauge sectors. Moreover, we provide estimates of electric dipole moment constraints and constraints from dark matter experiments.

Our research involves analyzing a pressurized cylindrical shell that is bent into a tube with a specified radius and attached to fixed ends with longitudinal tension applied. By incorporating a parameter that represents the mechanical properties of the material and the effects of pressure, we've calculated the stability of this structure under various conditions including a scan of the tension variable and the parameter governing material properties. This analysis also explores the utility of an approximation method for designing stables structures utilizing cane tubes and examines how the Cane-Blast experimental setup could be adapted for this analysis. Additionally, we've identified areas of research that could be informed by an experimental investigation of the stability of cane tubes.

In various fields, ensuring decision policies align with defined safety criteria, even when accounting for uncertainty, is a pressing concern. The former can be safeguarded against the latter through robustness guarantees obtained via credential Bayesian networks and their corresponding posterior bounds in probabilistic circuits. However, the practical limitations of such networks in regards to circuit size and depth hinder their scalability. This research addresses these issues by introducing an innovative approach that employs a high-level synthesis paradigm to simplify the circuit structure, effectively reducing its complexity and enabling more efficient computation of robustness certificates. The proposed method enables more stringent certainty assurances for existing systems and enables the utilization of more sophisticated certainty assurance methods. The results are validated through experiments employing state-of-the-art Bayesian networks and circuit synthesis tools.

In 1929, Leonid Mandelstam and Mikhail Leviar proposed an idea where a wave's steady flow could be converted into a temporal oscillation when it travels through a medium with varying frequency. This concept has since been observed in various systems: electric, atomic, and acoustic waves. We provide an overview of a different type of wave oscillation, which occurs in elastic media stimulated by high-frequency sound waves. This process can be seen as wave accumulation in a bragg reflector or as a result of the "winding" up of a wave plane in a medium with changing acoustic density.

In a generalised quadrangle, a code is a subset of the vertices with its minimum distance at least three. The elements of this subset are divided into distinct sets based on their distance from the code. Given a code in this context, its spreading density, partial spreading density, and neighbour-transitive index are calculated by determining certain ratios. The quadrangles' group action on the quadrangle's elements and the code's neighbour-transitive index are studied, leading to a proof that in a quadrangle with a transitive group, the spreading density, partial spreading density, and neighbour-transitive index are all one. Additionally, this proof leads to a corollary stating a specific property when a generalised quadrangle's group becomes transitive over the quadrangle's elements. The study also delves into the existence of two-element codes with specific distances in a quadrangle and further classifies all generalised quadrangles with a neighbour-transitive code of size four. The study also explores the existence of two-element codes with specific distances in a quadrangle and further classifies all generalised quadrangles with a neighbour-transitive code of size four.

We've analyzed the spatial structure of the Central Molecular Zone in the Milky Way's center using a two-dimensional correlation function to quantify its density pattern. By applying an anisotropic density model, we found evidence supporting the assumption that the Central Molecular Zone exhibits a more compact distribution along the diagonal than the perpendicular direction. We discovered distinct density patterns at various angular ranges and identified a critical angle of approximately 45 degrees where the density's isotropic properties become evident. Using a straightforward model, we determined the Central Molecular Zone's density pattern follows a Gaussian distribution at larger scales, but revealed a more complex pattern at closer distances. By analyzing the variability in our findings, we concluded that the 3D spatial structure of the Central Molecular Zone is too complex to be understood through two-dimensional research.

X-ray Absorption Near Edge Spectroscopy (XANES) provides a precise understanding of the local electronic structure of materials when combined with atomic-resolution microscopy. However, XANES data are sensitive to high-fluence damage caused by intense X-ray beams, which limits sensitivity and precision at the atomic level in large biological molecules. Researchers face an alternative in analyzing groups of electrons rather than individual ones and developing models that can accurately represent both damaged and undamaged electronic structures. A rate-based model of electron groups has been introduced and applied to human melanin proteins using simulations of linear and non-linear XANES data. This model supports time-dependent changes in electronic groups by facilitating communication between adjacent groups and outside sources. It is observed that electron group representations can be utilized to model distinct types of damage and that only certain conditions result in notable changes in XANES data. Using this model with modulated X-ray intensity reveals non-linear responses to increased fluence levels. The ability to model non-linear responses offers a more accurate understanding of how high-fluence damage affects XANES data and allows for the development of more robust denoising algorithms, thereby enhancing the analysis of atomic-scale local electronic structures.

A microtemperature detector incorporating an integrated temperature sensor was proposed, featuring a novel NMQB-based temperature-sensing voltage regulator. With the output of a reference cell serving as a thermistor, the design fulfilled the requirements for a BJT-based temperature-sensing circuit. Furthermore, the analysis revealed that the detector's temperature coefficient could be corrected by mitigating the influence of the Q-point's location on the detector's output. By utilizing a 0.6V to 1.8V input voltage range, the detector demonstrated a 0.24 degrees Celsius resolution and an error margin of $\pm$1.4 degrees Celsius. Moreover, the detector's energy consumption was measured at 1.06 nanajoules per conversion cycle.

Quantum entanglement serves as a cornerstone for quantum information science and technologies. Emphasizing the importance of entanglement creation and manipulation, this study introduces a novel method for generating polarization entanglement between two atoms using an optical fiber. The method utilizes an optical pulse to create an entangled state, which is then manipulated into a target entangled state using a quantum projection technique. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method and examine its practical implications in a real-world quantum system affected by decoherence.

This research paper explores the concept of digital geometry and spanners in the binary domain. It defines digital spanners and Euclidean spanners in the binary domain and investigates the relationship between their minimum vertex spanner ratio and the doubling dimension of a pointset. Additionally, the paper specifies the doubling dimension based on the binary Euclidean distance function and proves it is equivalent to the minimum number of segments needed to approximate a ball in the binary domain.

Accurate classification of IoT devices is a critical requirement, whether it's achieving energy efficiency or complying with data protection laws by pinpointing security breaches. However, current methods used to identify IoT devices often rely on comprehensive datasets which are frequently not available due to transportation costs or are too costly to obtain. This research introduces a new approach that minimizes costs by selecting the most effective features from a reduced dataset, also exploring the impact of sample sizes on accuracy to prevent excessive sampling. This innovative method leverages a unique combination of techniques: K-means clustering for feature grouping, multi-class logistic regression for model development, and a new cluster-based evaluation metric to optimize feature selection. Comparative tests confirm the efficiency of this method in reducing costs and pinpointing the optimal number of features.

Godel modal logic's sound and complete proof system is established through the integration of a Kripke semantics with a duality-based algebraic approach. This integration surpasses a traditional Kripke semantics model in several ways. Furthermore, the method used to establish the proof system's soundness and completeness can be applied to certain extensions of Godel modal logic.

This research presents a novel and straightforward method for word-alignment
that leverages bilingual extraction patterns identified in external sources.
These patterns can be applied to monolingual data without prior training,
enabling quick and efficient word-alignment within a data-driven
machine-translation system. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this
method using real-world examples of bilingual extraction patterns derived
from Wikipedia links and user-generated content on Reddit.

We've developed a distorted resolvent algorithm for finding Nash equilibria in various situations. By exploring the distorted resolvent approach established by Svaiter, we show its application in solving finite zero-sum matrix games, leading to an efficient numerical method that outperforms the Chosen Value algorithm. Furthermore, we use this algorithm to tackle finite mean-field games and quasi-convex functions without a Lipschitz constant, achieving better results in both cases.

I have expanded the calculations in Section 4 of the paper "New calculations for Primordial Black Hole Dark Matter halofraction as a function of threshold mass bias" by translating the calculations into a publicly available code, then applying it to various scenarios, such as using multiple PBBH masses to satisfy both galaxy and stellar data, or using advanced PBBH merger rates derived from simulated signals in GW150914. Furthermore, I have calculated PBH densities under several new constraints, whereas the original paper primarily focused on the overall dark matter density, this new code, called `pbh_code`, enables comprehensive studies, allowing users to choose their own PBH mass functions, matter/ radiation ratios, and other parameters to predict the PBH density as a fraction of total dark matter.

We conducted research into systems at equilibrium consisting of uniform wedge-shaped molecules using Monte Carlo simulations, exploring the effects of two types of molecules with different shapes and varying wedge angles. In the case of molecules with a 60-degree wedge angle, we observed two-phase regions consisting of ordered crystalline phases with 2-Monge and 3-Monge unit cells, respectively. When molecules without a 60-degree angle were used, an additional phase with saddle-shaped features emerged in the phase diagram. This phase did not occur in systems where molecules with a 60-degree angle were used and exhibited some similarities to a pentagonal ice structure.

This work investigates multivariate Gaussian time series with cross-spectral densities that remain constant over time, analyzing their stationary properties and developing straightforward recurrence relations to calculate variance and correlation functions. We also provide numerical examples demonstrating the benefits of these recurrence formulas in capturing time-invariant characteristics of the time series.

A conventional approach to viewing an image involves illuminating it with light, which interacts with the image and scatters back to the observer as a result. However, the illuminating light obscures the image, which is a fundamental limitation. In this paper, we explore a different method that allows us to view an image without shining light on it, using undetected photons from a Michelson interferometer. By modulating the image and measuring the interferometer's output, we can calculate the image's amplitude, which corresponds to the optical field of the image. Since our method utilizes undetected photons, it can benefit from the principles of quantum measurement theory to enhance its performance while maintaining a single-pixel resolution.

The interaction between complex liquids and solid surfaces influences a wide range of phenomena and uses, but the lubricating properties of foams with various textures remain poorly understood. This research investigates how different textures of liquid foams interact with solid walls, with findings suggesting that the friction resulting from these interactions significantly depends on the texture's detailed structure. By examining both real and synthetic textures, researchers discovered that the frictional behavior of the foams is also sensitive to the distribution of liquid within the foam structure. This knowledge has the potential to improve the precision of computer simulations modeling complex liquid-surface interactions and shed light on the underlying physical processes governing frictional forces in textured foams.

This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer diagnosis. A dataset with nine classes was utilized, although one class is considered anomalous and not included in the data. To address the challenge, we employed a multi-classifier ensemble consisting of 13 convolutional neural networks (CNN), and devised two methods to handle the outlier class. Additionally, we proposed an intuitive diagnostic strategy utilizing metadata features and information theory to analyze the datasets' class structure. Our analysis revealed that the dermoscopy image features contained the most diagnostic information, followed by clinical information and patient age. Notably, we discovered that the outlier skin lesion type could be distinguished from normal classes via entropy calculations and outlier detection methods.

We carried out a high-resolution ARPES study on sodium and found that the observed enhancement of its electronic mass is slightly less than expected from earlier research. These findings amplify the need for theoretical models more advanced than the random phase approximation. Contrary to the hypothesis suggesting significant acceleration of the carriers due to their interaction with spin fluctuations, our results do not support this theory. Additionally, a comparison with previous electron loss data indicates that sodium's mass enhancement due to dipole-type electron-hole interactions is substantially less than its mass enhancement due to monopole-type interactions measured using ARPES.

Building on a previous research [J. Chem. Phys. 149, 204201 (2018)], we explore a brand-new approach to convert microcanonical ensemble data into a form suitable for analyzing equilibrated systems. The proposed method utilizes the fact that trajectories in a Hamiltonian system remain constant in phase space volume, despite fluctuations in energy. This property enables the transformation of trajectory data into a representation compatible with the microcanonical ensemble. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach for simulating free expansion dynamics, overcoming a major limitation of a previous method that relied on trajectory averaging to mimic the microcanonical ensemble. The new approach proves particularly useful in scenarios involving low temperatures or highly confined states. Additionally, we showcase the applicability of this method in analyzing equilibrium time-of-flight spectra.

This work uses a combinatorial approach to calculate Kontsevich weights for graphs associated with connection and curvature in symplectic manifolds with a specified structure. It also determines an explicit formula for a differential operator in the basis of graph symmetries.

We explore solitary waves known as "nanoptera," characterized by exponentially small oscillations, in two preloaded systems based on the Korteweg de Vries equation. The first model involves a preloaded string composed of a weakly nonlinear chain of particles, coupled with a flexible beam, while the second represents a preloaded rotating shaft, comprised of a weakly nonlinear chain of particles in a lab frame. Both analyses yield solitary waves with the same tail behavior, albeit with oscillations, by applying the Stokes phenomenon or "nanooscillations." These oscillations diminish as the domain of interest expands and can be interpreted as a superposition of a solitary wave and a traveling wave. A special case of solitary waves arises when the nanooscillations vanish, leading to solitary waves with no oscillations. Furthermore, we investigate the decay of a crack-singularite and its corresponding tail behavior in a preloaded rotating shaft.

A hypothetical cosmic collider offers a singular opportunity to observe primordial physics involving the early universe's quantum gravitational state.
The theory behind this collider specifies that any colliding quantum particles must be separated by at least the scale of their Compton wavelength.
Given this, the rates of cosmic collisions are significantly slower than terrestrial experiments, but the vast scale of the universe's size helps to compensate for this limitation.
The current research provides precise calculations for the normal modes of cosmological fluctuations, yielding the highest frequency that can arise from a given source, and describes how these fluctuations interact with the cosmic horizon during different phases of evolution.
The study estimates that collisions involving masses greater than $10^{-2}$ Jansky are too low to observe, but those with higher masses within the observable range can provide direct evidence for new physics.
The research offers a method to quantify any discrete spectral features emerging from these interactions, and such features should be visible up to a frequency of approximately $10^{10}$ Hz.
The study suggests that any features below a certain threshold at $10^{10}$ Hz will be obscured by the dispersion of light during the photon's journey from the point of collision.

Consider a graph of even order G and its square extended graph G^2. Research indicates that if an orientable closed surface contains a representation of G and a homeomorphic immersion of G^2, then a 2-vertex-connected subgraph of G exists which has a square-free complement. Furthermore, a specific class of graphs known as accordion graphs are also represented on this surface. It's discovered that these accordion graphs possess unique properties, such as ensuring the quartic circulant graph with the same edge-set as 2-vertex-connected, but this is not true for all graphs in this category. Research also finds that feasible pairings of G are equivalent to the feasible pairings of this subclass consisting solely of the accordion graphs. Additionally, a necessary and sufficient condition for a graph to be an accordion graph has been established. Finally, a characterization of accordion graphs has been found through comparison with a specific supraph and the characterization of their squares as a product of two circulant graphs.

Our research involves analyzing the behavior of a three-state quantum walk on a one-dimensional lattice with periodic boundary conditions. We discover that unlike the corresponding quantum system, the equivalent probability distribution does not adhere to a scaling law. We overcome this discrepancy by investigating the probability distribution's decay rate in the long-term context and establish a new scaling law. Moreover, our study explores the distribution's spatial spread and reveals a scaling law applicable across various walk steps. Finally, we extend our analysis to consider the impact of additional assumptions and constraints.

Vision Transformers (ViTs) are currently receiving more attention for self-supervised learning due to their superior performance in unsupervised and semi-supervised computer vision tasks. In this research, we discovered that ViT's self-supervised learning capabilities can be enhanced by extracting low-level visual features. These low-level features develop emergent properties that benefit learning high-level visual representations. We investigated how these features evolve and found that they share characteristics with elementary principles in art and design. These findings were confirmed by analyzing the visual characteristics of the features through both qualitative and quantitative methods. Additionally, we utilized various diagnostic tools to demonstrate that the emerging attributes contribute significantly to the success of ViT in self-supervised learning.

A new cosmological model is introduced, incorporating modified gravity and dissipation to explain the acceleration of the universe and its early state. The model utilizes the Barshdole-Buckdahl-Berglund-Berman equation to describe the universe's evolution and applies the Lyra metric to convert this equation into a manageable form. The resulting model of dark energy, which includes a viscous Inflationary universe, uses the Lavrelashvili et al. potential function to characterize the interaction between dark energy and dark matter. By analyzing the best-fit values of the model's parameters, we find that they are consistent with a wide range of observational data, including the shift parameter and the slope parameter, as well as the Hubble parameter. Our model is successful in explaining multiple phases of the universe, including the deceleration-acceleration transition and the phenomenon of lighter phases at early times.

We present a straightforward proof that in three or more dimensions, the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Euler equations has a critical issue in terms of stability, specifically when using Sobolev spaces and certain types of Besov norms it defines.

Recent breakthroughs with large language models have sparked interest in text-based creative tools, but current models often produce low-quality outputs that fail to incorporate essential creative elements provided in a prompt. This problem is linked to a stable creep issue, where a model fixated on pleasing users with non-essential details, instead of incorporating the vital elements. This research introduces the Stable Creator, a novel steering system that utilizes a part of the model's capacity to maintain a consistent semantic orientation within ImageNet Semantics Embeddings. By doing so, the Stable Creator effectively prevents the model from deviating into irrelevant topics of high visual complexity, thereby facilitating the incorporation of essential creative elements. Through experiments with diffusion models on image and text creation tasks, the effectiveness of the Stable Creator in producing high-quality outputs has been demonstrated. This approach can be utilized not just with large language models but a wide range of other creative models.

Deep learning models that utilize Bayesian methods for uncertainty estimation tend to show more consistent improvements when combined with other techniques such as data augmentation, PR-DQN learning, or loss minimization. We discovered that the predictive uncertainty of a Bayesian Neural Network (BNN) accurately measures the concealment of reversible image data and serves as a reliable objective function for training non-Bayesian models. Furthermore, utilizing BNN uncertainty in an adversarial training approach yields concealed images that are nearly indistinguishable from genuine images, achieving superior visual quality and reconstruction error rates compared to standard adversarial training. The proposed method has been rigorously evaluated on diverse image datasets, showcasing its robustness and versatility.

Our research focuses on the implications of the $J/\psi$ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. The $J/\psi$ decays into these states are constrained by the search for a gamma line in the energy spectrum of the $J/\psi$ particle observed in the e+e- collider environment. Assuming that the invisible matter carries dark matter responsibility, our analysis reveals that the diphoton decay branch of the dark matter is significantly impacted, with the $J/\psi$ data now limiting it more severely than the Large Hadron Collider does. Moreover, the $J/\psi$ data restricts the Wilson coefficients $C_S$, $C_P$, and $C_PS$ governing the interaction of dark matter with the Standard Model in the neutrino sector more extensively than the Large Hadron Collider does, with these coefficients now potentially accessible in future experiments. The study also demonstrates that the search for a gamma line in the $J/\psi$ data is particularly adaptable to modeling the interaction of dark matter with the Standard Model via a gauge boson. Furthermore, the analysis shows that the invisible decays of the $J/\psi$ scalar mesons into light dark matter and an Higgs boson are largely insulated from the constraint of the gamma line, but the dual-portal model displaying strong self-interactions is left intact by the $J/\psi$ data, with this model potentially being constrained instead by direct dark matter detection experiments

High-resolution images from the SDO and HMI telescopes have been analyzed to study the characteristics of magnetic bright points (MBPs). These features appear as small, bright patches in solar photosphere images, generally present in areas of high shear and shear-related structures. In this study, we examine the basic properties of MBPs, including their appearance, behavior, and distribution of sizes. To achieve this, we first obtain statistical data on the areas of MBPs, and then apply a two-part distribution model to fit this data. The resulting fits enable us to determine the mean parameters of the distributions, including widths and heights, as well as the relative proportions of the distributions. The findings of this study indicate that the sizes of MBPs follow a two-part distribution pattern, with smaller MBPs being significantly larger than predicted by the earlier one-dimensional Gaussian model. The broader distribution is estimated to contain the majority of MBPs, while the narrower distribution is found to be significantly peaked on the order of a few hundredths of a solar unit, indicating a substantial size variation among the larger MBPs. The broader distribution is observed to exhibit a strong correlation with the solar cycle, peaked at 0.35 solar units during both the ascending and descending phases, while the narrower distribution appears to be relatively unaffected by the solar cycle.

Human vision is capable of discerning object movement at very low levels of illumination, a phenomenon that becomes feasible due to the flexible response of the human visual system to light. By exploiting this adaptability, humans can perceive motion in low-frequency high-amplitude illumination patterns, even if the associated light levels are below the normal sensitivity threshold. Notably, such minimal films can be both monochromatic and colorful. Research has shown that certain computer models are able to detect movement in these films, although only through the use of non-standard image processing methods. This study examines how human vision handles the processing of motion in minimal films, using both subjective testing and theoretical models, with the aim of determining the most effective detection approach.

Dark particles interacting with magnets through a kinetic term can strengthen the intracluster magnetic fields by transferring energy from cosmic rays generated in the Early Universe. We explore the possibility of dark matter consisting of magnetic monopoles having milliscale charges, which interact with standard matter only through magnetic forces, thus avoiding all other Standard Model interactions. Such a dark matter scenario offers two main benefits: it resolves the charge anomaly in the Universe, and it provides a natural explanation for the enduring presence of large-scale magnetic fields. Calculations indicate that, even after the Universe's electrons and photons decouple, cosmic rays retain sufficient energy to maintain pre-existing magnetic fields within galaxies and their clusters. Furthermore, interactions with dark monopoles prevent the collapse of magnetic fields in galaxies and galaxy clusters, thereby explaining the observed patterns of magnetic field strength and size. We estimate that dark monopoles weigh between 10^-11 and 10^-14 eV, which is consistent with the observed rotation curves of galaxies, while predictions for the Sun's interaction with galactic dark matter fall within previously established bounds.

The multiple time series problem of accurately forecasting the weather's impact on the power grid is extremely challenging. This paper proposes the Spatiotemporal Weather Forecasting (STWF) problem, aiming to predict weather conditions 12 hours in advance for 9 specific locations with 3 hourly time steps. To address the STWF problem, a novel Transformer-based framework, called TFOC, is developed. This framework leverages the Transformer's self-attention mechanism in three distinct contexts: the first forms a compact and distributed weather representation by aggregating the weather of 9 locations over the past 36 hours; the second applies a horizontal shift to its input sequence. The third utilizes a horizontal and vertical shift to its input sequence. In addition to the traditional self-attention, TFOC incorporates an aspired distribution representation using a Cross-Attention mechanism in three different orientations. Finally, TFOC exhibits a hierarchical time-unfolding structure with three levels of unfolding at the time step level. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that TFOC surpasses 11 existing baselines, 7 pre-trained models, and 8 robust transformer models, and showcases remarkable stability and data generalization capabilities.

In models that expand on the electroweak sector, a portion of the dark matter candidate's mass may arise from the vacuum expectation values of the involved fields, making it eligible to be fully stabilized by a confining gauge boson. Developing upon recent work of the authors [Phys. Rev. D 102, 055030 (2020)], this study incorporates a vectorial Higgs doublet and analyzes the dark matter candidates in three-Higgs-doublet models possessing $S_3$ symmetry, where one vectorial doublet gives rise to a fully stabilized scalar dark matter candidate and a fully stable fermion candidate, respectively. By leveraging the Dirac equation, the fully stable fermion's mass is completely generated in this framework, making it a naturally stable dark matter candidate. Furthermore, our analysis covers the case in which the fully stable fermion is not an absolute stable particle but instead exhibits long-lived properties. In this scenario, the fully stable fermion may endure away from the confinement of the gauge boson and, as a result, has a chance to decay into the scalar dark matter and a standard model Higgs boson. Our analysis is primarily based on the constraints imposed by the dark matter's relic density as measured by the XENON1T experiment, along with a consideration of the existing search for long-lived particles in the ATLAS experiment.

The PPT quadrilateral conjecture holds that any bipartite entanglement witness which is in a PPT state must indicate a genuine entanglement. We examine local operations that preserve PPT and maintain bipartite structure, discovering that a specific thermal state is invariant under any such operation, where the associated operator forms a Hilbert-Schmidt decomposition. In contrast to the PPT quadrilateral conjecture, a counterexample can be created where local operations on one system transform a PPT state into a non-PPT state on the other system. This counterexample also shows that the PPT quadrilateral conjecture is not preserved under the condition of equality in partial transpose entropy. Where the PPT quadrilateral conjecture does hold in the case of equal systems, a proof can be found referencing the method of matrix sums. Additionally, a PPT triangle conjecture is introduced and proven for the case of systems with three parties.

In living organisms, the nervous system's functioning relies on the intricate balance between the transportation of molecules within neurons, as evidenced by the severe consequences of imbalances caused by diseases such as Alzheimer's and Huntington's.  To better comprehend the complex processes governing molecular transport, we introduce a novel optimization model that accounts for the efficient movement of proteins along neuronal fibers.  By leveraging a combination of theoretical and practical approaches, we develop strategies to solve this complex problem, which mirrors real-world traffic congestion phenomena.  Throughnumerical simulations based on real neuronal geometries, we demonstrate the model's capacity to investigate the effects of environmental factors, like clogs, and identify optimal solutions to ensure smooth protein transport.  By combining this model with machine learning techniques, we enhance the resolution of transport profiles, enabling more accurate predictions.  Furthermore, we utilize Bayesian optimization to conduct thorough investigations of parameter sensitivities at a lower cost.  Through our study, we provide a comprehensive framework for analyzing the optimal conditions promoting healthy molecular transport in neurons.

The field of computational finance involves complex time-series data analysis in financial markets, which can be tricky to interpret. Analysts struggle to turn data into actionable information, leading many to seek novel data representations. This research introduces Network-maps of the MOOC (e.g., finding NEMo: fishing in finance networks using network motifs), which maps financial time-series data into a secondary, binary network. By utilizing network motifs, NEMo captures the inherent patterns within each time-series series. By comparing pairs of time-series, the mAD distance measures their similarity. Pairs with a minimal distance are considered highly similar, while those with the maximum distance are deemed dissimilar. The goal is to use NEMo to identify financial time-series binaries, which can be used in computational finance for detection purposes, such as identifying fraudulent activity or detecting financial anomalies. Preliminary results using real-world financial data demonstrate the potential of the NEMo approach, which is to group related time-series binaries based on their similarity. The used dataset contained weekly prices for S&P 500 companies from 2000 to 2010. The binary NEMo data consisted of 238 time-series, each representing a company, translated into a 238x238 matrix. The matrix was divided into four equal quadrants, representing four distinct market phases. The distance between pairs of time-series was used to create binary groups, which reflected the various phases. The methodology revealed companies sharing similar trends across the different phases, which aligns with financial analysts'

This research focuses on the emission patterns resulting from a white dwarf's (WD) fall towards a black hole (BH). We've developed a mathematical equation to describe the WD's accretion process and its associated energy spectrum. This model applies the concepts of general relativity and includes a traditional accretion physics framework. By simulating various mass ratios between the WD and BH, our findings indicate that a WD's mass must be significantly less than the mass of our sun to facilitate accretion. Moreover, we observed that energy released as gravitational waves is negligible compared to the spectrum emitted in the ultraviolet and gamma-ray ranges. This model predicts a broad spectral distribution that could be analyzed using existing X-ray spectroscopy methods to determine the WD and BH masses.

Three-body $\tau$-decays, which involve semileptonic interactions with light hadrons, can be examined using the hadronic component of the weak current. Studies of these decays have discovered entries in the vector and axial vectors of the weak interaction that don't align with standard model predictions. Certain decay processes with specific final hadronic states can be analyzed through precise calculations of hadronic radiative decays or by comparing the obtained form factors with those of established $e^\pm$-decay processes. This presentation will discuss recent findings from a three-body $\tau$-decay calculation that involves a light vector meson and includes the determination of hadronic radiation spectra.

Jim\'enez, Becerra, and Gelbukh (2013) introduced the "symmetric Tversky ratio models" with parameters $S_{\alpha,\beta}$ where $\alpha$ ranges between $0$ and $1$ and $\beta$ is greater than $0$. The inverse of each $S_{\alpha,\beta}$ function, denoted as $D_{\alpha,\beta}$, represents a semimetric for all possible subsets of a given set. Our research found that when $\alpha$ is $0.5$, the function reduces to the Jaccard distance, a well-known measure of similarity. Conversely, when $\beta$ equals $0$, the function $D_{\alpha,\beta}$ acts as a metric. We also showed that if $\alpha$ is greater than $0.5$, the function $D_{\alpha,\beta}$, for any given set, has a direct relationship with the normalized information distance between two elements in that set.

Modern image de-blurring methods based on deep learning have demonstrated superior performance compared to traditional techniques, but their effectiveness heavily relies on having sharply captured images or those with well-defined passwords. These methods fail when applied to blurry images or password protected content. To overcome these limitations, a novel approach employs a conditional image generator to create synthetic blurred images from clear ones, allowing non-noisy and password-protected content to be processed. By using pairs of clear and non-noisy human images or scene content as training data, the system learns to produce non-noisy synthetic human or scene sequences, which are then used in a dual training framework. This framework enables both a motion de-blurring network and a pseudo-blur synthesizer to optimize each other, ultimately enabling the deployment of state-of-the-art motion de-blurring method on single image inputs, including password-protected content. Experimental results show that the proposed method achieves superior performance on both human and scene sequences.

In the field of Molecular Electronic Systems, the connection between chemical networks and electrical circuits is of great importance. This work explores chemical networks that mimic the functioning of electrical circuits used in artificial neural networks, specifically those employing the spike-based learning algorithm known as STDP. This algorithm enables synapses to modify their connections according to the temporal relationships between spike occurrences. By utilizing the chemical equilibrium of reaction networks, the study demonstrates that the conditions for stable operation under the Siegel-Rosenberg condition can be met. This condition ensures robust adjustment of chemical concentrations in response to changes in reaction rate and feedback inhibition. Numerical analysis of the results, achieved through autonomous chemostats, confirms the capability of designing molecular systems that emulate spike neuron learning through artificial synapses.

The concept of extent in a ordered set refers to the greatest size of a sublattice within that set. This value can be represented as the supremum of the sizes of chains generated by a fixed element in the set's ultrapower. These chains are formed using an ultrafilter and an ordering induced from the original set. Similar to how cardinality applies to sets, extent applies to lattices and plays a significant role in lattice theory. This paper explores how extent is affected by an ultrafilter in the context of lattices and their ultrapowers, specifically examining cases where the extent of the original set and its ultrapower are comparable. We also introduce novel methods for generating chains in the ultrapower using a sublattice of a given lattice. A fundamental question arises - for any lattice of a given cardinality, does it have an sublattice of a smaller cardinality within it. Here, we provide answers to this question for combinatorial lattices and their ultrapowers. Additionally, we investigate the properties of lattices in ultrapowers relative to their position in Bochner diagrams.

Scientific breakthroughs in data-driven science increasingly rely on applying sophisticated AI models to comprehensive datasets, yet understanding how these models interact with specific datasets remains in its embryonic stages. Unlike the extensive analysis of AI model performance, dataset profiling is grossly underdeveloped, causing difficulties in pinpointing the sources of models' failures and optimising them with target datasets in mind. We make the case for dataset-specific profiling by illustrating the benefits it can bring to various stages of the data science pipeline and demonstrating the feasibility of a systematic approach to dataset profiling through the development of a profiling tool for Python, which we comprehensively evaluate across a wide range of datasets.

Hadwiger's conjecture asserts that every graph with $n$ vertices includes a minor of size $k$, where $k$ is equal to $n$ or more than $n-1$. This has been validated for graphs with 4 and 5 colorations. We demonstrate that if a graph $G$ has more than $n-5$ vertices and contains two distinct subgraphs of size 5, then it includes a minor of size 5. This confirms Hadwiger's conjecture for 5-chromatic graphs. We apply the same approach to verify the conjecture for 4-chromatic graphs by showing that if a graph $G$ has more than $n-4$ vertices and contains two distinct subgraphs of size 4, then it includes a minor of size 4. We use the concept of list colorings to analyze the size of the smallest possible minor in such graphs as well as the total number of possible list colorings for a given graph size. We calculate that if a graph $G$ has $n$ or fewer vertices, then the number of possible list colorings is less or equal to $5.95^n$. We use the results to prove that if a graph $G$ has more than $n-5$ vertices, then the number of possible list colorings is greater than $4.41^n$. We calculate that if a graph $G$ has more than $n-5$ vertices, then the number

This research introduces an advanced kernel-based graph signal reconstruction method using the generalized correntropy framework, aiming to improve the reliability of the traditional graph signal reconstruction equation. The study's initial finding indicates that optimizing the kernel width in the generalized correntropy-based graph signal reconstruction equation is a critical step in enhancing its performance. Building on this discovery, a novel algorithm is proposed, which estimates the kernel width adaptively by maximizing a related function and subsequently utilizes this estimate in the generalized correntropy-based graph signal reconstruction equation. The proposed algorithm is named the robust adaptive generalized correntropy-based smoothed graph signal reconstruction algorithm (RAGS-GSR). The performance of RAGS-GSR is compared to existing methods through both theoretical analysis and experimental testing, with simulation results showing its superior noise-resistance capabilities and more accurate signal estimates. Additionally, time complexity and data efficiency of RAGS-GSR are examined.

The entangled spinor Bose-Einstein condensate plays a crucial role in achieving record-breaking precision in the measurement of the phase shift in matter-wave interferometry. This achievement stems from optimizing the quantum state preparation in entangled spinor Bose-Einstein condensates to counteract detection limitations. A quantum state customization approach is introduced, allowing researchers to design the quantum state based on specific detection capabilities and desired outcomes. This method is demonstrated in the context of an atomic interferometer, where customizing the entangled spinor Bose-Einstein condensate leads to a significant and practical improvement in phase shift precision. Furthermore, our approach enables the translation of existing experimental results into high-precision values, demonstrating its practical utility.

The focus of this research is on non-linear, second-order elliptic operators with a wide range of applications across physics and engineering. Specifically, we establish precise estimates for the first eigenvalue of such operators subject to a particular boundary condition. This work builds on previous findings regarding the linear variant of these operators and has implications in the study of non-linear Navier-Stokes equations.

Deep Neural Network structures like the Graph Convolutional Neural Network (GCNN) excel in machine learning tasks for nodes in graph-based datasets, but their success hinges on an understanding of how they work. The graph convolution operation is the core of GCNN and has been explained in complex mathematical terms, but a crucial aspect of its interpretation has been overlooked - what unique characteristics of connected nodes allow the GCNN to accurately perform tasks? A proposed method refines this understanding by developing an intuitive matched filtering approach to reveal the basis of graph convolutionality. Empirical evidence also demonstrates that the matched filtering framework enables GCNNs to identify key graph features even in scenarios where the original definition is insufficient.

Despite the success of self-supervised learning, its application to dependency parsing has been hindered by a phenomenon known as "paragraph vector collapse" and by the high computational costs of sentence-level models. These challenges are exacerbated in settings of limited data availability. This research introduces a novel, self-supervised learning approach that addresses these obstacles, incorporating augmented self-contextualization and enhanced denoising objectives with a focus on dependency parsing specifics. By extending self-supervised learning to dependency parsing, it is possible to obtain more refined and robust parse trees compared to the existing state-of-the-art models when only unsupervised pre-training is employed. Furthermore, the developed method demonstrates its superiority over various baseline models in settings of either insufficient or partially annotated data.

We use the self-consistent light front quark model to calculate the transition form factors of the $B	o D\ell
u_\ell$ ($\ell = e, \mu, 
u$) semileptonic decays. The quark model contains three different dressings for the $D$ meson: the constituent quark model, instanton effects, and effects of vacuum polarization. The form factors obtained are then used to calculate the branching ratios of various $B	o D\ell
u_\ell$ decays. The calculated branching ratios are comparable to the experimental data, with the inclusion of vacuum polarization effects significantly improving the agreement between the theoretical predictions and the experimental data for the $B	o D\ell
u_\ell$ ($\ell = e, \mu$) decays.

Our findings suggest that quantum branes may develop when space-time symmetry operators violate time reversal symmetry due to a gap in the spectrum. We have found examples of such situations occurring within two-dimensional theories that combine gauge fields with Grassmann fields. In these cases, the gap in the spectrum arises from the difference in the dimensions of non-local symmetry operators that are hermitian but violate time reversal symmetry, and local symmetry operators that are quantum branes and adhere to time reversal symmetry. Furthermore, we have discovered that the spectrum gap generates a flow that stabilizes the time reversal symmetry, and the fixed point is characterized by a brane structure constant that represents the ratio of a key coefficient to a fundamental constant in the theory. We have also explored how the difference in dimensions affects a brane formulation of a gauge theory, causing a transformation of the brane charge when the charge is expressed in terms of the lattice regularization technique known as the NFQMC scheme.

Currently, Choiceless Polynomial Time (CPT) stands out as the most advanced query language for ordered structures, having surpassed even transitive closure in expressive power. A CPT-definable class therefore necessarily contains all definable by first-order logic (FOL) transformations of transitive closure, including those with parameters. A key feature of FOL definalbe transformations is their preservation of acyclicity, as demonstrated by Sagiv, Mearns, and Sharir's example involving the reachability relation in digraphs. A fundamental property of CPT definalbe transformations is also being closed under a specific form of acyclic digraphs. By utilizing these observations, it becomes possible to rigorously characterize the hierarchy of CPT definalbe acyclic digraphs and attain a new classification up to acyclicity. In the process, an even more advanced query language is developed which is capable of efficiently deciding reachability in a wider range of acyclic digraphs while only making a relatively small increase in computational complexity from $n^{O(\log \log n)}$ to $n^{O(\log n)}$.

In a compound known as pyrochlore zirconates, a specific series of substitutions brings about an insulator-to-metal transition, attributed to an effective reduction in spin-orbit coupling and the resulting formation of a large band gap relative to 2Bi. A comparable series of substitutions in pyrochlore iridates results in an insulating state at Eu$_{1-x}$Bi$_x$Ir2O7 ($x$ = 0.75, 0.50) but metallicity appears at $x$ = 0.25 of Bi doping. HXPES measurements in the current study indicate a significant reduction in Bi doping. The observed insulating state at $x$ = 0.25 Bi doping is attributed to an increased band gap due to the localized nature of Bi 6$s$ electrons and Bi-$d_{x^2-y^2}$ orbital lowering of the degeneracy of the upper Ir $j_{eff}=1$ triplets. Bi doping also results in Bi-$d$ electron bonding with Bi-$d$ orbital character in the metallic state at $x$ = 0.25 being significantly greater than at $x$ = 0.75. Our results in the Eu$_{1-x}$Bi$_x$Ir2O7 series reveal the degree of metallicity can be tuned by adjusting the degree of $d_{x^2-y^2}$ orbital lowering and final character of the valence band

Consider a metric space ${\mathfrak M}=({\mathcal M},\rho)$ and a Banach space $X$, with a set-valued mapping $F$ that maps ${\mathcal M}$ to the family ${\mathcal K}_m(X)$ of compact convex subsets of $X$ of dimension $m$ or less. Our recent joint research with S. Kolyadok [Kolyadok and Klatte, 2022] established a principle for selecting a Lipschitz continuous set-valued mapping $S$ from ${\mathcal M}$ to the family of closed half-spaces in $X$, such that for any $\beta\in(0,1]$ there exists an index $\kappa(F,\beta)$ such that for any $\rho$-(approximate) lipschitz selection $T$ of $F$ with parameter $\kappa(F,\beta)$, the difference between the Lipschitz constant of $S$ and $\kappa(F,\beta)$ is less than $\beta$. This theorem is a 2D analogue of a principle first demonstrated for Lipschitz selections of set-valued mappings from a metric space to the family of closed subsets of $X$ in \cite{Klatte2002}. In this paper, we provide a proof of a more general version of this theorem, in which the domain ${\mathcal M}$ is any complete metric space with Lipschitz diameter

The notion of nontransitive dice, which originated from a 1974 article by J.A. Gardner, has been developed into a concept applicable to general distributions via a formula for the likelihood of combinations. This concept led to identifying cyclic likelihoods. A specific class of nontransitive likelihoods was further defined and examples of this class were provided, demonstrating that this class constitutes a substantial portion of all nontransitive likelihoods. Moreover, a unique relationship between nontransitive likelihoods and probability measures on certain infinite spaces was discovered.

Software systems consistently experience disruptions, necessitating rapid adjustments to maintain operational continuity. Although compile-time tools can address these challenges, present solutions often fail to streamline run-time settings or require excessive compile-time input. This study investigates the potential of reducing run-time configuration complexity by shifting compatible settings to compile-time options. Our analysis involves a detailed examination of 15 software systems, including 7 package managers and 8 with compile-time defined configuration, across 3 programming languages. Our findings demonstrate that a substantial portion of run-time settings can be streamlined or optimized at compile-time, yielding significant benefits in both number of required settings and their complexity. Our online dataset is accessible at https://doi.org/10.24425/R1.2023.202039.

Light dark matter particles are most likely to interact with nuclei through the exchange of a virtual photon. This interaction can be modeled as an inelastic scattering process that results in the creation of an electron anti-electron pair. Direct detection experiments may be able to capture this scattering event by measuring the recoil energy of the nucleus, but the predicted signal is anticipated to be exceptionally faint. Alternatively, a more prominent signal can be obtained by recording the energy released directly from the electron. Although the direct detection of this interaction is hindered by high background noise from natural radioactivity, the experimental setup of a dual-phase xenon detector can be adapted to directly measure the electron's kinetic energy, thereby significantly enhancing the sensitivity to sub-GeV dark matter interactions. By doing so, current-generation detectors would be capable of searching for dark matter particles with cross-sections as low as 10^-31 cm^2, effectively closing the gap between current direct detection experiments and future ones.

This paper examines the behavior of a two-atom system in the anti-Jaynes-Cummings model, where one atom is irradiating a cavity and the other atom is in a cavity, coupled by radiation. We observe that the interaction between the atoms and the cavity results in the entanglement of the particles, as well as the transfer of energy from one atom to the other via Rabi oscillations. It is noted that the rate at which this energy is transferred can be modified and slowed down when the two atoms are strongly connected, due to the effects of entanglement. Moreover, the system's ability to transmit information efficiently can be affected by the environment for specific combinations of atomic states. We also investigate the long-term transmission properties of the system and find that efficient transmission only occurs under highly specialized conditions.

Measuring inter-beat intervals from ECG signals can provide early warnings for cardiovascular diseases. However, identifying IBIs from noisy signals is difficult, especially when they are heavily distorted by motion noise, which is common in individuals who are highly active. Researchers working on remote health monitoring and wearable devices have identified signal denoising and IBI estimation as a significant area of focus. Recent breakthroughs have involved the use of deep learning, with the study proposing the use of a Tiramisu model for this particular task. The model's results show notable improvements over existing approaches, with an increased overall accuracy of 0.5% and a significant reduction in error of 20.2%.

We derive three distinct forms of work performed by an active force on an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particle acting in two or three-dimensional space, and then extend our findings to a scenario in which the active force is accompanied by a thermal force with a different temperature. Our analysis also examines how these work expressions affect the particle's energy in the presence of active and passive Brownian motion in two and three-dimensional space.

This research introduces HUMBI, a large dataset featuring multiview sequences capturing human body gestures across various lengths. The dataset was captured using a high-resolution, advanced 3D human capture technology which provides detailed, wearable-based data equivalent to 300 frames per second, along with simultaneous facial and hand tracking. Our analysis reveals the high resolution enables accurate and efficient detection of intricate hand and finger movements. The dataset's value is further enhanced by the inclusion of diverse, target gesture classes related to multiple fields, such as psychology, sociology and medicine. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of existing state-of-the-art gesture detection algorithms using current dataset standards, comparing their performance to that achieved with traditional machine learning-based methods on HUMBI. Following the evaluation, we propose a new challenge: developing advanced, length-independent gesture detection algorithms capable of handling new, unseen gesture classes not provided during training. The HUMBI dataset and corresponding implementation are accessible at: \url{http://umini.com.hk/humbi/}.

Deep neural models have achieved significant cross-lingual transfer in NLP tasks by leveraging the training data available for a single language. However, this success heavily relies on extensive bilingual corpora being present. We introduce a model-agnostic approach that enables weakly supervised cross-lingual transfer using task representations as guidance. Since many NLP tasks lack perfect annotations, we utilize imperfect labels akin to noisey training data to adjust the model's parameters and facilitate transfer. Our experiments demonstrate that our method can effectively initiate learning for low-resource languages with imperfect labels and limited training data, and it successfully does so for both sentence and document-level tasks.

A robust video super-resolution approach called BasicVSR is recognized for its exceptional performance and user-friendliness, making it an ideal choice for establishing new video super-resolution benchmarks. However, certain limitations exist in its existing propagation and alignment components that hinder its further improvement. To address this, our research enhances BasicVSR by replacing its recurrent framework with a novel attention-driven propagation technique and refining its multi-head attention component for feature alignment. These enhancements empower BasicVSR to utilize more temporal information and accurately align smaller video features. Our results show that the improved BasicVSR achieves notable gains in PSNR and SSIM, surpassing the original version by approximately 0.40 and 0.30 dB respectively, with a minimal increase in its computational requirements of about 50%. Our implementation is publicly available at the GitHub repository https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/BasicVSR.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using a single unified model can be beneficial, but it can also suffer from catastrophic interference, where previous task learning severely hampers new task learning. This paper investigates how modular architectures, dividing tasks into separate sub-networks, handle interference in RL multi-task scenarios. By separating individual sub-networks or by adding modules incrementally, we show that modular architectures significantly mitigate interference and enable learning on previously unknown tasks without notable performance decline. Furthermore, we find that such modular approaches can replicate the benefits of double Baseline policies, but with significantly reduced requirements. This research confirms that modular architectures are well-suited for RL multi-task scenarios, effectively managing interference and achieving consistent performance across a range of challenging games and robotic tasks.

We have improved the performance of finite-time thermal engines using a
non-linear heat flux enhancement technique, which optimizes the heat
conduction rate based on real-time temperature differences between the
heat source and sink. This optimization is achieved by maximizing the engine
work over a finite time period and allowing the system energy for instantaneous
adjustments. The new technique is demonstrated with a prototype geometrical
model and reveals significant, optimal finite-time performance gains, thus
validating the technology for diverse thermally driven systems and even
micro-machines. Furthermore, this research paves the way for developing
advanced thermal management strategies in nanoscale devices and materials.

This research proposes a method for assessing the impact of hurricanes and storm surges on large power grids. To simulate the extreme weather scenarios, an agent-based model is used that accounts for spatial variations in hurricane and storm surge activity. This approach enables the derivation of probabilistic measures characterizing the severity of power disruptions. By conducting comprehensive investigations without specific power system details, this study evaluates the overall performance of different power transmission systems in relation to varying hurricane intensities and distribution patterns across a large power grid.

This paper explores a phenomenon akin to the Three Balls Theorem, notable in the context of Dirac operator eigenfunctions within the framework of Clifford analysis.
